books.title: Dragonflies!
books.art_why: Dragonflies are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Amazing Dragonflies Bzzt! You’re walking by a pond when something zooms past your head. It’s bigger than a bumblebee, and it’s faster than a butterfly. It’s an amazing dragonfly!
pages.brief: A dragonfly zooms past a child’s head beside a pond. The child is walking near the water, surprised by the fast insect. A bumblebee and a butterfly are nearby for size and speed comparison, with the dragonfly larger and quicker.

pages.text: What Are Dragonflies? Dragonflies are flying insects with long bodies and two pairs of wings. They come in every color of the rainbow. Some dragonflies have colorful stripes, and some even change color over time.
pages.brief: Several adult dragonflies with long bodies and two pairs of wings rest and fly near a pond. They show rainbow colors, including bright stripes, and one dragonfly appears in a different color to suggest color change over time.

pages.text: Young Dragonflies Dragonflies need water during every stage of their life cycle. Adults lay their eggs in water or on plants near water. The young dragonflies live in water for one or more years after they hatch.
pages.brief: A calm pond scene shows adult dragonflies laying eggs in the water and on plants beside it. Young dragonflies live underwater among the plants after hatching, staying in the water for one or more years.

pages.text: Young dragonflies look very different from adult dragonflies. They have gills inside their bodies, which allow them to breathe under the water. Dull green or brown coloring helps them hide from fish, frogs, and other hungry animals.
pages.brief: A close-up underwater view in a pond shows young dragonflies that look very different from adults. Their dull green or brown coloring helps them hide among plants from fish, frogs, and other hungry animals swimming nearby.

pages.text: As dragonflies grow, their skin doesn’t grow with them. Instead, young dragonflies shed their entire outer layer every time they need to grow. When a young dragonfly is ready to become an adult, it crawls out of the water. The last layer of skin splits open, and the adult dragonfly climbs out.
pages.brief: A young dragonfly crawls out of the water onto a plant stem. Its last outer layer splits open, and the adult dragonfly climbs out. Nearby, shed skins show how young dragonflies shed their entire outer layer whenever they need to grow.

pages.text: Super Sight Adult dragonflies have the largest eyes of any kind of insect. Each eye is made up of about thirty thousand tiny pieces. Dragonflies’ super eyesight, which allows them to see in almost all directions at once, helps them catch prey.
pages.brief: An extreme close-up shows an adult dragonfly’s head and its huge compound eyes, made of many tiny facets. The eyes fill much of the face, showing how the insect can see in almost all directions at once while it hunts prey.

pages.text: Amazing Flight Dragonflies can speed up faster than the world’s fastest race cars! Dragonflies are among the world’s fastest flying insects. Large dragonflies reach speeds greater than 22 miles (36 km) per hour.
pages.brief: A large adult dragonfly flies low over a pond, wings blurred with speed. A race car on a track in the background hints at how dragonflies can speed up faster than the world’s fastest race cars and fly among the fastest insects.

pages.text: Unlike most flying insects, dragonflies control each wing on its own. This skill lets them swoop and dive like fighter jets. They can fly forward, backward, and even upside down. Do You Know? Scientists study dragonfly flight to learn how to make better airplanes and helicopters.
pages.brief: An adult dragonfly swoops and dives over a pond, each wing angled on its own. It flies forward and upside down. In the background, an airplane and a helicopter stand on an airfield, suggesting scientists study dragonfly flight to make better aircraft.

pages.text: Amazing Hunters Adult dragonflies are high-speed flying hunters. They surprise mosquitoes and other small insects by attacking from behind and below. They kill their prey with a fast, powerful bite. Dragonflies often eat their catch without bothering to land.
pages.brief: A high-speed adult dragonfly with wings spread hunts above a pond, attacking a mosquito from behind and below. It catches the small insect in midair with a fast, powerful bite and eats its catch without landing.

pages.text: Dragonflies for Dinner Many animals like to eat dragonflies— birds, lizards, frogs, spiders, and even other dragonflies. Dragonflies’ flying skills help them avoid danger. Not many animals can catch these speedy insects. Humans eat dragonflies, too. In many parts of the world, dragonflies are a special treat. You can buy dragonflies on sticks for a snack.
pages.brief: A dragonfly flies above a pond while a bird, lizard, frog, spider, and another dragonfly watch. Nearby, a person holds dragonflies on sticks as a snack, showing that humans in many parts of the world eat dragonflies too.

pages.text: Swarms Dragonflies sometimes travel in huge groups, called swarms. They travel in swarms for food and to go south for the winter.
pages.brief: A huge group of dragonflies, called a swarm, fills the sky over open land as they travel together. The swarm moves for food and to go south for the winter, with many dragonflies flying close together.

pages.text: A Safe Place for Dragonflies In 1985, people in Japan created the world’s first dragonfly park. Today there are also dragonfly parks in Europe and the United States. Dragonflies are amazing creatures—and people all over the world are starting to realize it! Dragonflies Worldwide There are nearly three thousand kinds of dragonflies. They are found all around the world, in almost every kind of habitat. Check out your closest stream, pond, or lake. See if you can spot them for yourself!
pages.brief: Visitors walk through a sunny dragonfly park with a pond, stream, and lake, watching many dragonflies. Around them are different habitats where nearly three thousand kinds of dragonflies live worldwide, from the first park in Japan in 1985 to parks in Europe and the United States.

books.title: Eiffel Tower
books.art_why: The Eiffel Tower is a real place that exists today and can be photographed.

pages.text: A Famous Structure The Eiffel Tower is a structure that reaches up to the sky! The tower is famous. People around the world know about it. Almost seven million people visit the tower each year.
pages.brief: A tall metal tower reaches up to the sky in a city. Many visitors from around the world stand near its base and look up. The Eiffel Tower is famous, and almost seven million people visit it each year.

pages.text: High and Mighty The Eiffel Tower is made of four long beams of metal. At the bottom, the beams are the four legs of the tower. The beams curve up and meet at the top. When the Eiffel Tower was built, it was the tallest structure in the world.
pages.brief: Four long metal beams form the Eiffel Tower. At the bottom, the beams are four legs. They curve upward and meet at the top. The tower stands tall against the sky, shown as the tallest structure in the world when it was built.

pages.text: Paris FRANCE City on the Seine The Eiffel Tower is in Paris, which is the capital of France. The tower is much taller than other structures in Paris. It is at one end of a large park. The Seine (SEN) River flows next to the tower. Many museums, gardens, and ponds are nearby.
pages.brief: The Eiffel Tower stands in Paris, the capital of France. It rises much taller than the other structures around it. At one end of a large park, the tower stands beside the Seine River, with museums, gardens, and ponds nearby.

pages.text: A Tower of Strength Gustave Eiffel and three other men worked together on the idea for the Eiffel Tower. A contest was held to get ideas for a special structure for the 1889 World’s Fair. The men won the contest. It took many workers about two years to build the tower.
pages.brief: Gustave Eiffel and three other men work together on an idea for a special structure. They enter a contest for the 1889 World's Fair and win. Later, many workers build the tower over about two years.

pages.text: The Eiffel Tower was built out of more than eighteen thousand pieces of iron. Iron is a type of metal. Mr. Eiffel wanted to prove that metal is as strong as stone.
pages.brief: More than eighteen thousand pieces of iron make up the Eiffel Tower. The pieces are a type of metal. Mr. Eiffel stands among the pieces, wanting to prove that metal is as strong as stone.

pages.text: First, stone and cement were placed in the ground. Next, the small pieces of iron were put together to make the large beams. Then, workers put the beams on top of the stone and cement. The tower grew taller and taller.
pages.brief: First, workers place stone and cement in the ground. Next, they put small pieces of iron together to make large beams. Then workers set the beams on top of the stone and cement as the tower grows taller and taller.

pages.text: Here to Stay Long ago, structures were not as tall as they are today. Many people thought Mr. Eiffel could not build such a tall tower. Other people thought the tower would be ugly. When the Eiffel Tower was finished, it was beautiful!
pages.brief: Long ago, structures are not as tall as they are today. Many people think Mr. Eiffel cannot build such a tall tower, while others think the tower will be ugly. When the finished tower stands complete, it is beautiful.

pages.text: Mr. Eiffel wanted to make the tower useful to people so it would stay standing for many years. He put a science lab in the tower. Many people came to use the lab. Later, people used the tower to send radio and TV signals. The first French radio station with news and music began in 1921. It sent signals from the tower.
pages.brief: Mr. Eiffel wants the tower to be useful so it will stay standing for many years. He puts a science lab inside, and many people come to use it. Later, people use the tower to send radio and TV signals; in 1921 a French radio station sends news and music from the tower.

pages.text: Visiting the Tower Take a ride in a glass elevator to the top of the Eiffel Tower. The city of Paris looks amazing from that high! The second floor has shops, restaurants, and displays about how the tower was built. The first floor has a see-through floor. There is also ice-skating every winter.
pages.brief: A glass elevator carries visitors to the top of the Eiffel Tower, where the city of Paris looks amazing far below. The second floor has shops, restaurants, and displays about how the tower was built. The first floor has a see-through floor and ice-skating every winter.

pages.text: The Eiffel Tower doesn’t always look the same. Workers paint it every seven years, and sometimes the color changes. The tower has been dark red, dark yellow, and brown at different times. It’s always huge and amazing!
pages.brief: The Eiffel Tower does not always look the same. Workers paint it every seven years, and sometimes the color changes. At different times the tower has been dark red, dark yellow, and brown. It is always huge and amazing.

pages.text: Lighting Up the Sky In 2004, the Eiffel Tower’s lights were red for the Chinese New Year. In 2006, the lights were blue for another holiday. They were green and gold for a big sports contest in 2007. The tower had a special show of lights and fireworks to welcome the year 2000. Something fun is always happening at the tower!
pages.brief: The Eiffel Tower lights up in different colors. In 2004 the lights are red for the Chinese New Year. In 2006 they are blue for another holiday, and in 2007 green and gold for a big sports contest. A special show of lights and fireworks welcomes the year 2000.

books.title: Adding It Up
books.art_why: Real cubes, children, animals, zoos, and ranches can all be photographed.

pages.text: There are many ways to find the answers to addition problems. You can find answers by using: • cubes • your fingers • paper and pencil • mental math You are going to practice all of these ways to solve addition problems. Problem: On his farm, Mr. Patel raises chickens, turkeys, ducks, and geese. He has twenty-three birds in all. If he buys four ostriches, how many birds will he have on his farm?
pages.brief: Mr. Patel stands in a farmyard with chickens, turkeys, ducks, and geese around him. Twenty-three birds are visible in the yard, and four ostriches stand nearby. Cubes, fingers, paper, and a pencil are arranged nearby to suggest different ways of adding.

pages.text: How many birds will Mr. Patel have if he buys four ostriches? Try using cubes to solve. 1. He has twenty-three birds now. Count twenty-three blue cubes to show this. How many tens do you have? How many ones? You have 2 tens and 3 ones. 2. He will buy four ostriches. Count four single orange cubes to show the ostriches. Now you can find the total number. You have 2 tens and 7 ones. You have twenty-seven cubes. Answer: Mr. Patel will have twenty-seven birds in all.
pages.brief: A child arranges twenty-three blue cubes into two groups of ten and three single cubes. Beside them, four orange single cubes stand for the ostriches. The child then counts all the cubes together and sees two groups of ten and seven singles, making twenty-seven cubes in all.

pages.text: You can use cubes in another way to find the total number of birds. 1. Just say the starting number, twenty-three. You don’t have to show twenty-three with cubes. 2. Lay out four cubes to show the four ostriches. 3. Use the cubes to count on from twenty-three. There will be twenty-seven birds in all.
pages.brief: A child says the starting number, twenty-three, without showing it with cubes. Four cubes lie on a table to stand for the four ostriches. The child points to each cube and counts on from twenty-three, reaching twenty-seven. The farmyard birds and ostriches appear in the background.

pages.text: You can also use your fingers to find the total number of birds. 1. Say the starting number, twenty-three. 2. You are going to add four to twenty-three. Use your fingers to count on from twenty-three. You can write an addition sentence to tell what you did. There will be twenty-seven birds in all. Riddle: When is it hard to count on using your fingers? Answer: If you are adding more than ten, you’ll run out of fingers! 23 + 14?
pages.brief: A child counts on from twenty-three using fingers, adding four more. A pencil and paper rest nearby. The child looks at a riddle about counting on with fingers when adding more than ten, imagining running out of fingers. The farm birds and ostriches remain in view.

pages.text: Problem: Isaac’s class is doing a project on reptiles. The children take a class trip to the Reptile House at their city’s zoo. They count forty-seven snakes and lizards. Then the class goes to the turtle pond. They count eight turtles. How many reptiles have the children seen in all? You have two numbers, or addends, 47 and 8. Try using cubes to find the sum. 1. Count out forty-seven blue cubes to show the snakes and the lizards. Make as many tens as you can. You have 4 tens and 7 ones.
pages.brief: Isaac’s class visits the Reptile House at the city zoo. The children count forty-seven snakes and lizards in glass enclosures. At the turtle pond, they count eight turtles. Beside the zoo scene, forty-seven blue cubes are grouped into four tens and seven singles to show the snake and lizard count.

pages.text: 2. Count out eight red cubes to show the eight turtles. 3. It’s easier to add from a ten. So, make another ten using the single blue cubes and the single red cubes. This is called bridging a ten. Answer: There are fifty-five reptiles at the zoo.
pages.brief: The children count eight red cubes for the eight turtles. They use single blue and red cubes together to make another ten, bridging a ten. The cubes now show fifty-five reptiles in all. In the background, the zoo’s Reptile House and turtle pond hold snakes, lizards, and turtles.

pages.text: You can also count on your fingers to solve. 1. There are forty-seven snakes and lizards. Start with forty-seven. 2. You have to add eight turtles. First, add enough ones to get from forty-seven to fifty. It can help to find the total when you bridge a ten. 3. You have used three of the eight to make ten. Think: How many of the eight are left? 8 – 3 =? 8 – 3 = 5. There are five left. 4. Add the remaining five turtles. There are fifty-five reptiles.
pages.brief: A child starts with forty-seven snakes and lizards, then adds eight turtles using fingers. The child first uses three to reach fifty, then adds the remaining five. The fingers show fifty-five reptiles. Nearby, the zoo Reptile House and turtle pond appear with the counted animals.

pages.text: Problem: Owl Hill Ranch has six horses. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. How many horses are there at Tall Pine Ranch? This problem is different from the first two problems. Read it carefully! Be sure to answer the question that is asked.
pages.brief: Two ranches are shown side by side. Owl Hill Ranch has six horses gathered near a fence. Tall Pine Ranch has a larger herd, thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. A child studies the two ranch scenes carefully, ready to answer the question asked.

pages.text: Cubes can help you picture the information and find out how many horses are at Tall Pine Ranch. 1. Start with what you know. There are six horses at Owl Hill Ranch. Use six green cubes to show those six horses. 2. Tall Pine Ranch has six horses plus thirteen more. Use six orange cubes to show those six horses. 3. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. Count thirteen more orange cubes to show all the Tall Pine Ranch horses.
pages.brief: A child uses cubes to picture the horse information. Six green cubes stand for the six horses at Owl Hill Ranch. Six orange cubes show the same six horses at Tall Pine Ranch, and thirteen more orange cubes are added to show the thirteen extra horses there.

pages.text: 4. Now you need to add the two sets of orange cubes. Here is one way. You add thirteen orange cubes to that number. First, add the ten to the six. Then, add the remaining ones. You have six orange cubes. Adding is easier if you make a ten. You can also draw a picture to help you solve. Owl Hill Tall Pine +13 Answer: Tall Pine Ranch has nineteen horses.
pages.brief: A child adds ten orange cubes to six, then adds the remaining three ones, making a ten. A simple drawing of the two ranches lies nearby to help solve. The cubes and drawing show Tall Pine Ranch with nineteen horses. The green cubes for Owl Hill Ranch stay in view.

pages.text: Problem: Josh loves cats. He has cats on his wallpaper. He has cats on his bedspread. He has cat posters. He has one real cat, too! Josh also has a lot of books about cats. Josh loaned his friend Natalie nine of his books to read. Josh still has twenty-six cat books. How many cat books did he have before he loaned Natalie nine books? You know how many cat books Josh has now. You know how many he loaned Natalie. You don’t know the starting number. Think about this problem. Josh loaned nine books. He still has twenty-six books. To find the starting number, you need to add nine and twenty-six.
pages.brief: Josh sits in a room filled with cat wallpaper, a cat bedspread, cat posters, and many cat books. His one real cat rests nearby. Natalie holds nine cat books that Josh loaned her. Twenty-six cat books remain with Josh, and the picture shows him thinking about how many he had before.

pages.text: You can draw a picture and count the total. Josh has a total of thirty-five books. You also may be able to solve this problem in your head. Think: 26 + 9 can be hard to add. 26 + 10 is easier. 26 + 9 is one less than 26 + 10. Natalie Answer: Josh started out with thirty-five books.
pages.brief: Josh draws a picture of books and counts the total, reaching thirty-five cat books. He also thinks in his head: twenty-six plus nine is one less than twenty-six plus ten. Natalie stands nearby with the nine books she borrowed. The cat-themed room and Josh’s real cat remain in view.

pages.text: Problem: Owl Hill Ranch has six horses. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. How many horses do both ranches have in all? How is this problem different from Problem 3? Look back at page 9. In Problem 3, you needed to find out how many horses live at Tall Pine Ranch. For this problem, you need to find the total number of horses at both ranches.
pages.brief: The two ranches appear again. Owl Hill Ranch has six horses. Tall Pine Ranch has thirteen more horses than Owl Hill Ranch. A child looks from one ranch scene to the other, comparing this problem with the earlier one and thinking about the total number of horses at both ranches.

pages.text: Try using cubes to solve. Which group of cubes shows the horses at Owl Hill Ranch? Which group of cubes shows the horses at Tall Pine Ranch? Which group of cubes shows the total number of horses at both ranches? The addition sentence that shows what you did is 6 + 19 = 25. Check back at the cubes you chose. Did you choose correctly? or or or.
pages.brief: A child sorts groups of cubes. One group shows six horses at Owl Hill Ranch, another shows nineteen horses at Tall Pine Ranch, and a third shows twenty-five horses at both ranches together. The child checks the cube groups, choosing the one that matches the total.

pages.text: Here are two other ways to solve the problem. Try solving 6 + 19 in your head. Think: 19 is about 20. There are twenty-five horses in all at both ranches. What pictures could you draw to solve this problem? Riddle: Can you think of a way that you could use your fingers to solve 6 + 19? Turn the page upside down for the answer! Answer: You could reverse the addends to get 19 + 6. Then count on from 19 with your fingers. Remember, you can add addends in any order. You’ll get the same total.
pages.brief: A child tries other ways to solve the horse problem. The child thinks that nineteen is about twenty, draws pictures of the horses, and uses fingers to count on from nineteen after reversing the addends. Twenty-five horses stand together at both ranches in the background.

books.title: The Animal Data Files
books.art_why: Real zoo animals, children, and data charts can be photographed today.

pages.text: Meet the Animals There are all kinds of animals at the County Zoo. The zoo has a Zoo Kids Club for children. Children in the club get to spend time at the zoo. They learn a lot about animals. Right now, they are helping to keep track of the zoo’s baby animals. From January to July, eight animal mothers had babies. Baby Animals Born at the County Zoo emu meerkat python tortoise armadillo swan camel opossum The emu is a giant bird that can’t fly. It can run fast, though. Emus are a lot like ostriches. The armadillo has bony plates of armor all over its body. This armor protects the armadillo from harm.
pages.brief: At the County Zoo, children in the Zoo Kids Club spend time near animal enclosures, watching and learning about baby animals. An emu, a large flightless bird, runs on strong legs. Nearby, an armadillo shows bony plates of armor covering its body. Eight animal mothers have had babies from January to July.

pages.text: The meerkat is a long, skinny, furry animal. A meerkat often stands all the way up on its hind feet. Its tail helps it to balance. The Burmese python is one of the world’s largest snakes. This python can be longer than four adults lying head to foot. The Galapagos giant tortoise lives longer than almost any other animal. This tortoise might live for more than one hundred years. The swan has webbed feet to help it swim. This bird’s neck is longer than its body. The camel is used to living in very dry lands. It can go for days without drinking water. The opossum is a small, furry animal. It carries its newborn babies in a pouch.
pages.brief: A meerkat stands upright on its hind feet, using its tail for balance. A long Burmese python stretches across the ground. A Galapagos giant tortoise rests nearby. A swan swims with webbed feet and a neck longer than its body. A camel stands in dry land. An opossum carries newborn babies in its pouch.

pages.text: Make a Tally The children use a tally to count the babies. Some of the babies were born. Others hatched from eggs. The children make a tally table to show their information. Tally Count means 1 Animal Mother Born or Hatched When Born or Hatched How Many opossum born January 8 python hatched February 20 emu hatched June 3 camel born April 3 armadillo born March 17 swan hatched June 10 Galapagos tortoise hatched May 11 meerkat born March.
pages.brief: Children make a tally table to count the zoo’s baby animals. Some babies were born, and others hatched from eggs. The children mark tally counts beside animal mothers such as opossum, python, emu, camel, armadillo, swan, tortoise, and meerkat, noting when each arrived and how many.

pages.text: Close-Up: All in the Family How many animals are born or hatched from a mother at one time? It depends on the kind of animal! • A zebra gives birth to just one foal at a time. • A camel gives birth to just one calf at a time. • A hummingbird usually lays two eggs at a time. • A polar bear usually has two to four cubs. • One kind of armadillo usually has four babies that are exactly alike. • Some rabbits have eight babies. • A duck can lay as many as twelve eggs. • An alligator might lay forty or fifty eggs. Not all of them will hatch, though. • Some snakes lay as many as one hundred eggs! They won’t all hatch.
pages.brief: A zebra stands with one foal, and a camel stands with one calf. A hummingbird sits near two eggs. A polar bear rests with two to four cubs. An armadillo has four babies that are exactly alike. A rabbit is with eight babies. A duck sits on as many as twelve eggs, while an alligator and a snake have many eggs.

pages.text: Make a List The kids can use the data they have gathered in different ways. Data is information in the form of numbers. The data can show which babies were born or hatched first. The kids put the data in a list. Birthdays of the Zoo’s Animal Babies January 8—opossum’s babies born February 20—python’s eggs hatched March 8—meerkat’s babies born March 17—armadillo’s babies born April 3—camel’s baby born May 11—tortoise’s eggs hatched June 3—emu’s eggs hatched June 10—swan’s eggs hatched The list is arranged in time order. It shows the order in which the babies were born or hatched.
pages.brief: Children gather data about the zoo’s baby animals and put it in a list. They arrange the birthdays in time order, starting with the opossum’s babies in January, then the python’s eggs, meerkat, armadillo, camel, tortoise, emu, and swan through June.

pages.text: Close-Up: Time to Hatch • Once an emu lays her eggs, the eggs take about 55 days to hatch. • A Galapagos tortoise’s eggs can take as long as 130 days to hatch. • A swan’s eggs hatch in about 35 days. • A python’s eggs hatch in about 60 days. Egg-Hatching Times for Other Animals hummingbird—11–16 days pigeon—about 17 days crane—about 30 days duck—about 30 days ostrich—about 40 days.
pages.brief: An emu sits on eggs that take about 55 days to hatch. A Galapagos tortoise’s eggs may take as long as 130 days. A swan’s eggs hatch in about 35 days, and a python’s eggs in about 60. Nearby, a hummingbird, pigeon, crane, duck, and ostrich each sit with their eggs.

pages.text: List by Groups The data can show whether more bird babies, mammal babies, or reptile babies were born or hatched during this time. The kids sort their data by the class of animal. Classes are one way that scientists group animals. There are five classes of animals with backbones. They are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. The zoo animal mothers belong to three of those five classes. The kids write the number of babies instead of showing tally marks. Numbers are easier than tally marks to read quickly. Birds Mammals Reptiles.
pages.brief: Children sort the zoo baby data by animal class. They write numbers instead of tally marks to show how many babies belong to birds, mammals, and reptiles. The zoo animal mothers fit into three of the five vertebrate classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.

pages.text: Close-Up: Three Classes of Animals with Backbones Birds: Birds hatch from eggs. All birds have feathers. They are the only animals with feathers. All birds have wings, but some birds do not fly. Reptiles: Most reptiles hatch from eggs, but some are born live. Reptiles have scaly skin. Their body temperature changes with the outside temperature, so they can’t live in very cold places. Mammals: Nearly all mammals are born live, not hatched from eggs. Most mammals have fur or hair. Mammal mothers produce milk to feed their babies.
pages.brief: A bird hatches from an egg and shows feathers and wings. A reptile with scaly skin rests in a warm place; most reptiles hatch from eggs, though some are born live. A mammal mother, covered in fur, feeds her babies milk. These examples show birds, reptiles, and mammals—three classes of animals with backbones.

pages.text: Make a Pictograph The data can show when the greatest number of babies were born or hatched. The kids re-sort data from page 5 to make a pictograph showing which month the most babies were born or hatched. A pictograph uses icons, or pictures, to stand for what is being counted. The key shows how many items each icon stands for. Animal Babies Born or Hatched Each Month To find the number for each month, read across a row. Skip-count by twos. You can also compare amounts by looking at how long each row is.
pages.brief: Children make a pictograph from their animal-baby data. Small pictures stand for the babies born or hatched each month. The children read across each row, skip-count by twos, and compare row lengths to see which month had the most babies.

pages.text: Close-Up: Heart to Heart • Your heart beats about 90 times each minute. • A camel’s heart beats about 28 times a minute. • An elephant’s heart beats about 30 times a minute. • A gray whale’s heart beats only about 9 times a minute. • A cat’s heart beats about 120 times a minute. • A mouse’s heart beats about 500 times a minute. • A hummingbird’s heart beats as many as 1,200 times a minute!
pages.brief: A person’s heart beats about 90 times each minute. A camel’s heart beats about 28 times, an elephant’s about 30, and a gray whale’s only about 9. A cat’s heart beats about 120 times, a mouse’s about 500, and a hummingbird’s as many as 1,200 times each minute.

pages.text: Make a Bar Graph The kids present the same data another way. A bar graph uses bars instead of icons to show amounts. On a bar graph, you can find how many by looking at the number scale at the left of the graph. You don’t need to count. How to Read a Bar Graph for the Exact Number Animal Babies Born or Hatched Each Month • Read the labels to see what data the graph shows. • Find the top of each bar. • Look left to find the number at which the bar ends. Number of Babies Jan Feb Mar Apr May June Month Notice that the number scale starts at zero!
pages.brief: Children present the same animal-baby data as a bar graph. Bars of different lengths show the number of babies born or hatched each month. The children find each bar’s top and look left to the number scale, which starts at zero, to read the exact amount.

pages.text: Close-Up: Wing and Feather Facts • Penguins use their short, strong wings for swimming, not flying. • Bats are the only mammals with real wings. But their wings are covered with skin, not feathers. • The bones of flying birds are very light. In fact, all of a flying bird’s bones might weigh less than all of its feathers. • Feathers are made of keratin. This is what our hair and nails are made of. Number of Feathers Some Birds Have sparrow—about 3,500 bald eagle—about 7,000 swan—about 25,000.
pages.brief: A penguin uses short, strong wings to swim. A bat shows wings covered with skin, not feathers. A flying bird has very light bones. Feathers are made of keratin, like hair and nails. A sparrow, bald eagle, and swan display their feathers, with the swan having about 25,000.

pages.text: Your Turn! Now you try collecting and showing data. Collect the data that answers the questions below. Then place the data in the list and tally table on the next two pages. • In what months were your friends born? • How many teeth have each of your friends lost? Close-Up: Teeth or No Teeth A grown person has 32 teeth. You have about 24 teeth. How does this number compare with the numbers of some animals? • A hippo has about 44 teeth. • A camel has 34 teeth. • Some armadillos have just 28 teeth. But the giant armadillo has as many as 100 teeth. How would you show the data about teeth? • The long-snouted spinner dolphin has as many as 252 teeth. • An opossum has 50 teeth. • Birds have no teeth at all.
pages.brief: Children start collecting their own data, asking friends about birthday months and lost teeth. A grown person has 32 teeth and a child about 24. Animal teeth are compared: a hippo, camel, armadillo, long-snouted spinner dolphin, opossum, and a bird with no teeth at all.

pages.text: Write each of your friends’ names next to the correct month in the table. My Friends’ Birthday Months Months Friends January February March April May June July August September October November December.
pages.brief: Children write each friend’s name next to the correct month in a birthday table. The table has spaces for January through December, and the children fill in friends’ names beside the month in which each friend was born.

pages.text: Write each of your friends’ names in the column on the left. Use a tally to write the number of teeth they have lost in the column on the right. Friend Number of Teeth Lost Number of Teeth Lost by My Friends.
pages.brief: Children write each friend’s name in the left-hand column. In the right-hand column, they use tally marks to show how many teeth that friend has lost. The page gives a place for each friend and a tally count for lost teeth.

books.title: Discovering Dinosaurs
books.art_why: Dinosaurs lived long before photographs existed, so their world cannot be shown in a real photo.

pages.text: Finding Fossils How do we know dinosaurs lived on Earth? Scientists discover fossils in rocks all over the world. Studying fossils helps them learn about dinosaurs. They study what dinosaurs looked like, where they lived, and what they ate.
pages.brief: Scientists examine fossils in rocks in different places around the world. They study the fossils to learn what dinosaurs looked like, where they lived, and what they ate. The scene shows scientists at work with rocks and fossil remains, helping them understand dinosaurs.

pages.text: Fossils are the remains of plants or animals from long ago that have turned to stone. Scientists have found many different types of dinosaur fossils, including bones, footprints, teeth, nests, and eggs.
pages.brief: Fossils are remains of plants or animals from long ago that have turned to stone. Scientists have found many kinds of dinosaur fossils, including bones, footprints, teeth, nests, and eggs. The picture shows examples of these fossil types together, with scientists studying the remains.

pages.text: These scientists out of the ground. After wrap them to keep them safe. Then the scientists will take them to a museum. Scientists will study the fossils. They’ll examine the shape and color of the fossils. They’ll also consider where the fossils were discovered and how deep underground they were discovered.
pages.brief: Scientists dig fossils out of the ground. After they find them, they wrap the fossils to keep them safe. Then the scientists take the fossils to a museum. At the museum, scientists study the fossils, examining their shape and color and considering where and how deep underground they were found.

pages.text: Scientists can sometimes fit bone fossils together to form a complete skeleton. Most dinosaurs had hundreds of bones, so it is difficult to find all of them. Scientists use other dinosaur skeletons to help them piece together the fossils and understand the missing bones.
pages.brief: Scientists fit bone fossils together to form a complete skeleton. Most dinosaurs had hundreds of bones, so finding all of them is difficult. Scientists use other dinosaur skeletons to help piece together the fossils and understand the missing bones. The scene shows scientists assembling bones into a dinosaur skeleton.

pages.text: Learning from Fossils Although dinosaurs are extinct, the skeletons of other animals help scientists understand dinosaur skeletons. Some dinosaur bones may be bigger than those of animals alive today. However, many are still shaped the same.
pages.brief: Although dinosaurs are extinct, skeletons of other animals help scientists understand dinosaur skeletons. Some dinosaur bones may be bigger than bones of animals alive today, but many are still shaped the same. The picture shows scientists comparing dinosaur bones with skeletons of animals that live today.

pages.text: Many different types of dinosaurs roamed Earth. Scientists study fossils to learn how dinosaurs moved around. Some dinosaurs walked on two or four legs, and some used wings to fly.
pages.brief: Many different types of dinosaurs roamed Earth. Scientists study fossils to learn how dinosaurs moved around. Some dinosaurs walked on two legs, some walked on four legs, and some used wings to fly. The scene shows several kinds of dinosaurs moving in different ways.

pages.text: As dinosaurs moved around Earth, they left tracks behind. Scientists study fossil footprints to learn how fast or slow dinosaurs moved. Footprints also give clues about how big or small the dinosaur leaving the tracks might have been.
pages.brief: As dinosaurs moved around Earth, they left tracks behind. Scientists study fossil footprints to learn how fast or slow dinosaurs moved. Footprints also give clues about how big or small the dinosaur that left the tracks might have been. The picture shows scientists examining fossil footprints on the ground.

pages.text: Scientists study fossil teeth to learn about the diets of dinosaurs. Many dinosaurs grew new teeth to replace those they had worn down or lost. Some dinosaurs had razor-sharp teeth that helped them cut through meat or plants. Others had flat teeth that they used to grind their food.
pages.brief: Scientists study fossil teeth to learn about dinosaur diets. Many dinosaurs grew new teeth to replace teeth they had worn down or lost. Some dinosaurs had razor-sharp teeth for cutting through meat or plants. Others had flat teeth for grinding food. The scene shows scientists looking closely at different fossil teeth.

pages.text: Scientists learn about dinosaur babies from fossil nests and eggs. Dinosaur eggs came in many different shapes and sizes. Some dinosaurs laid over twenty eggs at a time, while others laid only a few eggs. Like birds, some dinosaurs may have sat on their nests until their eggs hatched.
pages.brief: Scientists learn about dinosaur babies from fossil nests and eggs. Dinosaur eggs came in many different shapes and sizes. Some dinosaurs laid over twenty eggs at a time, while others laid only a few. Like birds, some dinosaurs may have sat on their nests until their eggs hatched. The picture shows fossil nests and eggs.

pages.text: Scientists find fossils of plants, fish, insects, and other animals in the same rocks as dinosaur fossils. These fossils help them learn what Earth was like when dinosaurs lived here. It’s also easier for scientists to find the age of the other fossils than dinosaur fossils. The other fossils are more complete than dinosaur fossils. They’re also found more often. Scientists can estimate the age of dinosaur fossils based on the age of the other fossils.
pages.brief: Scientists find fossils of plants, fish, insects, and other animals in the same rocks as dinosaur fossils. These fossils help them learn what Earth was like when dinosaurs lived. The other fossils are easier to date and are more complete and found more often. Scientists estimate dinosaur fossil ages from them. The picture shows these fossils in rocks.

pages.text: How Long Ago? Scientists can do tests to determine the age of fossils. Older fossils are found in rocks deep in the ground. Newer fossils are discovered in rocks closer to the surface. The oldest dinosaurs lived around 230 million years ago.
pages.brief: Scientists do tests to determine the age of fossils. Older fossils are found in rocks deep in the ground. Newer fossils are discovered in rocks closer to the surface. The oldest dinosaurs lived around 230 million years ago. The scene shows fossils in rock layers at different depths, with scientists testing them.

pages.text: Scientists aren’t sure how or why dinosaurs disappeared 65 million years ago. Studying dinosaur fossils helps scientists look for clues to understand what happened.
pages.brief: Scientists are not sure how or why dinosaurs disappeared 65 million years ago. Studying dinosaur fossils helps scientists look for clues to understand what happened. The picture shows scientists examining dinosaur fossils and thinking about the disappearance of dinosaurs.

books.title: Jack-o'-Lanterns
books.art_why: The book includes an old Irish fable and historical origins, so some scenes cannot be photographed.

pages.text: What Is a Jack-o’-Lantern? Carved pumpkins are called jack-o’- lanterns. Jack-o’-lanterns are used to decorate for Halloween. People started carving jack-o’-lanterns more than a hundred years ago. At first, people didn’t carve pumpkins. They used other vegetables instead.
pages.brief: Several carved pumpkins with glowing faces decorate for Halloween. In a scene from long ago, people carve faces into other vegetables instead of pumpkins, showing that jack-o’-lantern carving began more than a hundred years ago.

pages.text: An old fable from Ireland may tell how people began carving jack-o’-lanterns. The fable is about a man named Stingy Jack, who liked to play tricks on everyone. When he died, he was cursed to walk in darkness forever. He carved a turnip and put a light inside. His ghost was known as “Jack of the Lantern,” and then “Jack-o’-lantern.”
pages.brief: In an old Irish fable, Stingy Jack, a man who likes playing tricks, carves a turnip and puts a light inside it. After he dies, his ghost walks in darkness forever, carrying the glowing turnip and becoming known as Jack-o’-lantern.

pages.text: Modern Jack-o’-Lanterns The Stingy Jack fable later became part of a night called All Hallows’ Eve. In Europe, people lit fires and dressed up to keep away ghosts.
pages.brief: In Europe, people light fires and dress up in the dark to keep ghosts away during All Hallows’ Eve, the night that later became Halloween. The old Stingy Jack fable became part of this night.

pages.text: In Ireland and England, people carved scary faces on vegetables and placed a light inside. All Hallows’ Eve later became known as Halloween.
pages.brief: In Ireland and England, people carve scary faces into vegetables and place a light inside each one. These glowing carved vegetables are shown at night, and the celebration called All Hallows’ Eve later becomes known as Halloween.

pages.text: When jack-o’-lantern carving was brought to the United States, people started using pumpkins. More than a billion pounds (more than 450 million kg) of pumpkins are grown in the United States each year.
pages.brief: In the United States, people begin using pumpkins for jack-o’-lanterns. A wide pumpkin field shows many pumpkins growing in the country, while people carve pumpkins, because more than a billion pounds are grown each year.

pages.text: Carving Jack-o’-Lanterns Carving pumpkins is fun for people of all ages. Smooth pumpkins work well for jack-o’-lanterns. Some people buy carving kits, while others carve without any help.
pages.brief: People of all ages carve smooth pumpkins at a table. Some use carving kits with special tools, while others carve their pumpkins without any help, enjoying the fun of making jack-o’-lanterns together in a group.

pages.text: First, with help from a parent, cut a hole in the top of the pumpkin to make a lid. Next, scoop out the inside flesh and seeds.
pages.brief: A child works with a parent to cut a hole in the top of a pumpkin and make a lid. Next, the child carefully scoops out the inside flesh and seeds from the open pumpkin.

pages.text: Draw a design on the pumpkin, and then carve it carefully. After the pumpkin is carved, place a candle or other light inside. Finally, put the pumpkin lid back on top.
pages.brief: Someone draws a design on the pumpkin and carves it carefully. After the carving is done, a candle or other light is placed inside, and the pumpkin lid is put back on top to glow.

pages.text: Jack-o’-Lantern Events Many cities have events to show off their carved pumpkins. In Hudson Valley, New York, jack-o’- lanterns make up a big display with spooky sounds and music. Pumpkins are used to make snakes, dinosaurs, and a dome carved with twinkling stars.
pages.brief: At a big display in Hudson Valley, New York, many carved pumpkins glow at night with spooky sounds and music for visitors. Pumpkins are carved into snakes, dinosaurs, and a dome decorated with twinkling stars.

pages.text: A huge display in Los Angeles, California, has pumpkin cars and dinosaurs. It also has pumpkin carvings of famous people. The artists carve their pumpkins at the event while people watch. Giant Jack-o’-Lantern An artist carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded. The pumpkin was as heavy as a cow! The artist beat his own Guinness World Record for largest jack-o’- lantern, which he had earned five years earlier.
pages.brief: In Los Angeles, California, a huge display shows pumpkin cars, dinosaurs, and carvings of famous people while artists carve and people watch. An artist carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded, a pumpkin as heavy as a cow, beating his own world record from five years earlier.

pages.text: A town in New Hampshire broke a world record for the most lit jack-o’- lanterns. The town had thirty thousand jack-o’-lanterns lit at once! Halloween Under the Sea People even display carved pumpkins underwater. Some aquarium workers put carved pumpkins in large ocean tanks each autumn for visitors to enjoy.
pages.brief: A town in New Hampshire shows thirty thousand lit jack-o’-lanterns glowing at once, setting a world record. Elsewhere, aquarium workers place carved pumpkins underwater in large ocean tanks each autumn so visitors can see them.

pages.text: The Tradition Continues Carving pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns is a fun holiday activity. However they are carved, jack-o’-lanterns are a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner.
pages.brief: A collection of jack-o’-lanterns carved in different ways glows brightly as a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner. People enjoy carving pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns as a fun holiday activity, and the tradition continues.

books.title: New Year Celebrations
books.art_why: Keyword check indicates drawing for these global tradition scenes.

pages.text: Introduction People around the world celebrate the New Year at different times of the year. They also celebrate the New Year in many different ways. Some people celebrate with parties. People have many different New Year traditions. Many people make New Year resolutions. A resolution is a promise to end a bad habit or begin a good one. It can be anything from cutting back on junk food to being a better friend.
pages.brief: Groups of people in different countries celebrate the New Year with parties and traditions. Some people write or think about a New Year resolution, promising to end a bad habit or begin a good one, such as eating less junk food or being a better friend.

pages.text: Eritrea Ethiopia Africa Enkutatash is the New Year celebration in the African countries of Ethiopia and Eritrea. It falls around September 11. The new year marks the end of the rainy season. People hold torches to look like the sun is shining. Families and friends eat together, drink coffee, and share gifts. Children often give daisies and make paintings.
pages.brief: In Ethiopia and Eritrea, families and friends sit together eating, drinking coffee, and sharing gifts. People hold torches outside at dusk so the light looks like sunshine. Children carry daisies and make paintings after the rainy season ends.

pages.text: Canada United States Mexico North America In the United States, around a million people come together on New Year’s Eve in New York City. They count down the seconds until midnight together. Then, the crowds cheer and celebrate. Many cities set off fireworks at midnight.
pages.brief: In New York City on New Year’s Eve, a huge crowd stands together at night, counting down the seconds until midnight. The people cheer and celebrate when midnight comes. Fireworks burst over city skylines in many cities.

pages.text: In the United States, special football games are played on New Year’s Day. Some people in Canada celebrate the New Year by jumping into freezing water. It is called a Polar Bear plunge. Do You Know? In the southern United States, people eat a dish made of rice and black- eyed peas. Some believe that if you enjoy simple foods on New Year’s Day, you might do well the rest of the year.
pages.brief: In the United States, football players play a special game on New Year’s Day in a stadium. In Canada, people jump into freezing water. In the southern United States, a dish of rice and black-eyed peas sits on a table for simple New Year food.

pages.text: Central and South America It’s good luck to eat twelve grapes on New Year’s Eve in Central and South America. Each grape stands for one month of the coming year. Cleaning your house CENTRAL AMERICA before midnight so SOUTH that good luck feels AMERICA welcome is also a popular tradition. People sweep out the old to start the New Year fresh.
pages.brief: In Central and South America, a person eats twelve grapes on New Year’s Eve, each grape standing for one month of the coming year. Nearby, someone sweeps a house clean before midnight, sweeping out the old to start the New Year fresh.

pages.text: At midnight, some people sweep in coins to bring wealth for the New Year. In many countries, people say goodbye to bad luck in another way. They throw water out of the window. Two-Faced! The month of January is named for the Roman god Janus. Janus was the god of doors, gateways, and beginnings. He is usually shown with two faces. One face looks backward at the old year. The other looks forward into the New Year.
pages.brief: At midnight, a person sweeps coins across a floor into a room to bring wealth. Elsewhere, someone throws water out of a window to say goodbye to bad luck. The Roman god Janus is shown with two faces, one looking back and one looking forward.

pages.text: Scotland Denmark Greece Europe In Denmark, people smash old and broken dishes on the doorsteps of family and friends. This brings them good luck in the New Year.
pages.brief: In Denmark, people carry old and broken dishes to the doorsteps of family and friends. They smash the dishes on the steps, leaving broken pieces at the doors to bring good luck in the New Year. Houses line a European street.

pages.text: In Greece, people bake a special cake with a coin hidden in it. If you get the slice with the coin, then you will have luck in the coming year! On New Year’s Eve, people in Scotland carry torches and swing balls of fire.
pages.brief: In Greece, a family gathers around a special cake, and one slice holds a hidden coin. Whoever gets the coin slice will have luck in the coming year. In Scotland on New Year’s Eve, people carry torches and swing balls of fire outdoors at night.

pages.text: Thailand Cambodia Philippines Southeast Asia In the Philippines, round things stand for coins and good luck. People celebrate the New Year by wearing clothes with polka dots. They also eat twelve different types of round fruit.
pages.brief: In the Philippines, people wear clothes with polka dots to celebrate the New Year. On a table sit twelve different types of round fruit. Round coins and round shapes around them stand for coins and good luck in the coming year.

pages.text: In parts of Southeast Asia, the New Year in late March or mid-April. It’s a very hot and dusty time of year—a time for water festivals. To prepare for the New Year, people clean statues of the Buddha with water. They save the water. Then, the water is poured onto people’s shoulders to bring them good luck. Water Fight! In Thailand, the water festival is called Songkran. It usually lasts from April 13 to 15. Parade floats spray crowds with water. Children chase one another with water blasters and water pails. It is very hot in Thailand on New Year’s Day. A water fight is the perfect way to celebrate!
pages.brief: In Southeast Asia, people clean statues of the Buddha with water and save the water. They pour the saved water onto people’s shoulders to bring good luck. In Thailand, Songkran parade floats spray crowds with water while children chase one another with water blasters and pails in hot weather.

pages.text: Conclusion For some people, the New Year happens at a different time every year. The Islamic New Year is based on a calendar that follows the cycles of the Moon. The 365-day calendar is based on the time it takes for Earth to move around the Sun. The Chinese and Jewish New Years are based on both calendars.
pages.brief: People look at a Moon calendar and a Sun calendar side by side. One follows the cycles of the Moon for the Islamic New Year. Another shows Earth moving around the Sun over 365 days. Chinese and Jewish New Year calendars are based on both calendars.

pages.text: From fireworks to cleaning your house, people share many New Year’s traditions around the world. Most traditions help you begin the New Year with a fresh start and a fun celebration. How will you celebrate the New Year?
pages.brief: People around the world celebrate the New Year with fireworks in the sky and clean houses, smiling together. Most traditions help them begin the New Year with a fresh start and a fun celebration. A child looks happy, thinking about how to celebrate.

books.title: Spain
books.art_why: Modern Spain, its cities, people, food and landscapes are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: Map of Spain FRANCE PORTUGAL SPAIN MOROCCO Where Is It? Spain is a country in Europe. It lies south of a long mountain range. The country of France is on one side, and Portugal is on the other. A group of islands is also part of Spain. These islands sit off the coast, in the sea.
pages.brief: A wide map view shows Spain in Europe, with France on one side and Portugal on the other. Morocco is nearby. A long mountain range lies to the north. Spain's islands sit offshore in the sea.

pages.text: Madrid is the capital of Spain. More than three million people live there. The palace is one of its biggest buildings. It used to be home to the Spanish king and queen and their family. Today, the family lives in a much smaller palace outside Madrid.
pages.brief: Madrid is Spain's capital, home to more than three million people. A large palace stands among its biggest buildings. It once housed the Spanish king, queen and their family. Today the royal family lives in a much smaller palace outside Madrid.

pages.text: People About forty-eight million people live in Spain. Many people work at jobs in hotels and other places to take care of visitors. Other people grow olives or make cars and clothes.
pages.brief: About forty-eight million people live in Spain. Many work in hotels and other places that take care of visitors. Others grow olives or make cars and clothes. People are shown busy at these jobs across the country.

pages.text: Spain belongs to a group of countries that work together to solve problems. People in Spain speak Spanish. Sometimes they also speak another language.
pages.brief: Spain belongs to a group of countries that work together to solve problems. People in Spain speak Spanish. Sometimes they also speak another language. Spanish people are shown connected with this wider group of countries.

pages.text: Spain’s Landforms Land Most of Spain has mountains and high flatlands. Beautiful beaches line its coasts. The Pyrenees (PEER-uh-neez) mountains in the north make a border between Spain and France.
pages.brief: A broad landscape view shows mountains and high flatlands across most of Spain. Beautiful beaches line its coasts. In the north, the Pyrenees mountains make a border between Spain and France. They are a natural boundary.

pages.text: The mountains are 434 kilometers (270 mi.) long. They stretch from the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. Different animals, such as the bearded vulture, live in the mountains.
pages.brief: The Pyrenees mountains stretch 434 kilometers from the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. They form a long mountain chain. A bearded vulture flies high above the rocky slopes, where different animals live in the mountains.

pages.text: History Spain is very old. Long ago, people from different parts of the world moved there to live. The Romans built roads and bridges. Then, people from northern Africa arrived. They built a beautiful palace that still stands today.
pages.brief: Spain is very old. Long ago, people from different parts of the world moved there to live. The Romans built roads and bridges. Then people from northern Africa arrived and built a beautiful palace that still stands today.

pages.text: More than four hundred years ago, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ruled Spain. They made many important changes. They paid explorers like Christopher Columbus to sail on a ship and find riches for Spain. Today, the people of Spain choose leaders to rule the country. Spain still has a king, but he does not make the laws.
pages.brief: More than four hundred years ago, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ruled Spain. They made important changes. books.title: Rainbows
books.art_why: The book mixes myths, an old experiment and modern science, so drawn scenes fit the range.

pages.text: Introduction When the Sun shines after it rains, run outside, and you may see a giant rainbow sweeping across the sky. Sometimes you may even spot small rainbows indoors when sunlight shines through a window.
pages.brief: A child runs outside after rain while the Sun shines, looking up at a giant rainbow sweeping across the sky. Nearby, sunlight shines through a window indoors, making small rainbows on the floor or wall.

pages.text: Rainbows are illusions made by light. We can see them, but we can’t touch them or walk around them. Outdoor rainbows seem to move away when we go toward them. Rainbows appear when light shines through something clear like water. They are beautiful tricks of light, but science can explain the reasons behind the tricks.
pages.brief: A child walks toward a bright rainbow in the sky, but the rainbow stays far ahead. The child's hand reaches out toward the colors, showing it cannot be touched. Sunlight shines through clear water nearby.

pages.text: Where and When Rainbows Appear Look around the next time you see a rainbow—the Sun will be shining from behind you, and there will be rain in front of you. That is where you will see the rainbow.
pages.brief: A person stands outside with the Sun shining behind them and rain falling in front. A rainbow appears in the rainy sky ahead. The person looks toward the rainbow, showing where it can be seen.

pages.text: Rainbows need water drops and sunshine to form. Rainbows most often appear in the morning or late afternoon, when the Sun is in the best places to create one. You might even see a double rainbow.
pages.brief: Sunlight shines through falling water drops in the morning or late afternoon sky. A bright rainbow arcs across the sky, and a second, fainter double rainbow appears beside it. The Sun and rain are both present.

pages.text: You may see rainbows in the mist of a waterfall, too. A splashing fountain can also create a small rainbow. Rainbows can even form under a bright moon. These are called moonbows.
pages.brief: A waterfall sends mist into the air, and a rainbow appears in the mist. Nearby, a splashing fountain creates a small rainbow. At night, a bright moon shines and a faint moonbow forms in the dark sky.

pages.text: We usually see a rainbow as a half circle. It actually forms a full circle, but from the ground we can only see the top half. Sometimes, a lucky airplane pilot may see the complete circle of a rainbow from the sky. Rainbows in Myths and Tales • Vikings said a rainbow bridge linked their gods to Earth. • In Ireland, people tell fairy tales about pots of gold hidden at the ends of rainbows and guarded by elves. • The Hindu god Indra is shown using a rainbow as an archer’s bow to shoot lightning arrows.
pages.brief: From the ground, people see only the top half of a rainbow, a half circle. High above, an airplane pilot looks down at the complete circle. In myth scenes, Vikings see a rainbow bridge, Irish elves guard a pot of gold, and the Hindu god Indra draws a rainbow bow to shoot lightning arrows.

pages.text: How Rainbows Form Years ago, a French scientist decided to study rainbows. He used sunlight and a big globe of water to experiment. He found that to see a rainbow, a person must be looking at light from the right position.
pages.brief: A French scientist studies a rainbow using sunlight and a big globe of water. The scientist stands in the right position, looking at light passing through the water globe. The experiment shows how a person must look from the right place to see a rainbow.

pages.text: Understanding how light travels on land. Now to run through knee-deep water. You will move because it is denser, or thicker, than air. In the same way, light moves faster through air than through water. Light bends when it moves between water and air, which is why a pencil sitting in a clear glass of water looks bent.
pages.brief: A person runs through knee-deep water, moving more slowly because water is denser than air. Beside this, a pencil sits in a clear glass of water and looks bent. Light bends as it moves between water and air.

pages.text: Outdoor rainbows form when water drops meet sunlight. The light bends as it enters each drop. The light then reflects, or bounces, off the back of each drop, like light off a mirror. The light bends again as it leaves the drop. Light bends and bounces in millions of water drops at once. This process makes all the colors of a rainbow. 1 2 1 2.
pages.brief: Sunlight enters a water drop, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again as it leaves. Many water drops do this at once in the sky. The bending and bouncing light in millions of drops creates all the colors of a rainbow.

pages.text: The Colors of the Rainbow Sunlight is made up of many colors. We can see them when water drops split the light into different colors. To see a rainbow, you have to be in the right place. Each water drop reflects colored light at a slightly different angle. We can only see red light shining from the drops at the rainbow’s top. Those drops are in the right place to shine the color red back at us. In the same way, we can only see violet shining from drops at the rainbow’s bottom.
pages.brief: Sunlight splits into many colors as it passes through water drops. At the top of the rainbow, drops shine red light back toward a viewer. At the bottom, drops shine violet light. Each drop reflects colored light at a slightly different angle.

pages.text: The colors of a rainbow always appear in the same order. The name ROY G. BIV can help you remember the seven main colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Make Your Own Rainbow 1. Fill a clear glass about three-quarters full of water. 2. Place the glass where sunlight can pass through it. 3. Hold a white piece of paper so the light shines through the water onto the paper. Move the paper around until a rainbow appears. 4. Use colored pencils to mark the different colors on the paper. How many can you see? What order are they in?
pages.brief: A child fills a clear glass three-quarters full of water and places it where sunlight passes through. The child holds a white piece of paper so light shines through the water onto it, moving the paper until a rainbow appears. Colored pencils lie nearby.

pages.text: Conclusion For a long time, rainbows have been featured in art and stories from all over the world. Most people find it hard not to stop and stare when a rainbow appears. Science explains how these colorful displays happen. Water drops bend, split, and reflect light, allowing us to see the many colors of a rainbow. Still, the beauty of a rainbow is a magical sight to see.
pages.brief: People stop and stare at a colorful rainbow in the sky. Around them are artworks and storybooks from different places, showing rainbows in art and tales. The bright display hangs above, while water drops bend, split, and reflect light to make its colors.

books.title: Great Zimbabwe
books.art_why: The book describes an ancient city and its ruins from centuries ago, so a drawing fits the historical setting.

pages.text: An Ancient City The ancient city of Great Zimbabwe was once rich and powerful. Now the city is empty. Its ruins give us some clues about what life was like there. However, there are still many mysteries about the people who once lived there.
pages.brief: A wide drawing of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe as a once rich and powerful place, now empty stone ruins that give clues about life there, with a sense of mystery about the people who once lived in the city.

pages.text: Where Is It? The ruins of Great Zimbabwe are in the southeastern part of Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe is a country in southern Africa. It is north of the country of South Africa. It is west of Mozambique. Great Zimbabwe Great Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: A simple map of southern Africa showing the country of Zimbabwe and its neighbors, with South Africa to the south and Mozambique to the east, and the ruins of Great Zimbabwe in the southeastern part of Zimbabwe.

pages.text: Who Built It? At first, European explorers were not sure who built Great Zimbabwe. However, experts can now prove that local people built the great city. Both works of art and the way that the walls were built help prove this fact. Most people think that the builders were a tribe called the Shona. The word Zimbabwe is thought to mean “stone houses” in the Shona language.
pages.brief: European explorers look at the great stone walls with puzzled expressions, while experts study works of art and the way the walls were built to prove that local Shona people built the city and its stone houses.

pages.text: Building the Walls Builders used stone bricks to build the walls of Great Zimbabwe. First, they split huge rocks in the countryside to make bricks.
pages.brief: The first step in building the walls is shown as builders in the countryside split huge rocks into stone bricks, working carefully to make the blocks used for Great Zimbabwe’s walls, with rocky ground around them.

pages.text: Then, they stacked the bricks to build high walls. They did not use anything to hold the stones together. However, the stones fit together tightly. The walls are well built. In some places, huge rocks form part of the walls. The walls of Great Zimbabwe are curved instead of straight.
pages.brief: Builders in Great Zimbabwe stack stone bricks into high walls without anything holding the stones together; the stones fit tightly, huge rocks form parts of the walls, and the walls curve instead of running straight.

pages.text: Three Areas The city has three main parts. The first is the Hill Complex, a large stone building on a hillside. This is the oldest area of the city. The kings of Great Zimbabwe may have lived here.
pages.brief: The Hill Complex, a large stone building on a hillside, is shown as the oldest area of Great Zimbabwe; kings may have lived there in the past, looking out over the city from the high stones.

pages.text: In the valley below, many smaller houses form the Valley Ruins. The houses were made of a mixture of clay and small rocks called daga. The people of the city lived in these houses. Across the valley is the Great Enclosure. Inside is a tall building in the shape of an oval. It is the largest ancient building in southern Africa and may have been a palace.
pages.brief: In the valley below, many smaller houses made of clay and small rocks form the Valley Ruins where people lived; across the valley stands the Great Enclosure with its tall oval building, the largest ancient building in southern Africa, perhaps a palace.

pages.text: Great Zimbabwe Hill Complex Valley Ruins Great Enclosure The walls of Great Zimbabwe were: • 11 meters (36 ft.) high in some places—as tall as a three-story building • up to 6 meters (20 ft.) thick in some places • very smooth in some places.
pages.brief: A tall, thick stone wall of Great Zimbabwe rises beside a three-story building for scale; parts of the wall are very smooth, and the Hill Complex, Valley Ruins and Great Enclosure are visible in the landscape around it.

pages.text: A Great City Great Zimbabwe was rich and powerful hundreds of years ago. The people raised crops and cattle. They also traded with other people from West Africa and the Middle East. They even traded with China, which is very far away from Great Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: In a busy scene, people of Great Zimbabwe raise crops and cattle near their rich and powerful city, while traders bring goods from West Africa, the Middle East and faraway China to trade, with animals and goods around them.

pages.text: However, after doing well for hundreds of years, the people left their city. They may have gone to find better farmland or better trade. Nobody knows for sure.
pages.brief: In an uncertain scene, after doing well for hundreds of years, the people leave their city behind; families walk away toward possible better farmland or better trade, though nobody knows for sure why they left.

pages.text: Mysteries Remain Scientists still have many questions about the ruins of Great Zimbabwe. For example, they do not know the purpose of some of its buildings. They also do not know why the people built the tall stone walls. Finally, there is the question of why the people left the city.
pages.brief: Scientists examine the ruins of Great Zimbabwe with questioning expressions, looking at buildings whose purpose is unknown and tall stone walls whose reason for being built is unclear, wondering too why the people left the city.

pages.text: The ruins of Great Zimbabwe have been damaged. People have stolen from the site. Wind, rain, and plants have caused problems. Laws protect the ruins, but more money and workers are needed to take care of the site. If the ruins are preserved, perhaps someday scientists can solve the mysteries of Great Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: The damaged ruins of Great Zimbabwe show stones disturbed, plants growing over walls, and signs of wind and rain; people have stolen from the site, and more money and workers are needed to preserve it for future study.

books.title: Colosseum
books.art_why: Ancient Roman life and the Colosseum games existed before photography, so drawings are needed.

pages.text: ITALY H.
pages.brief: A clean contents page for a book about the Colosseum. A small illustration of the ancient Roman arena appears beside a neat vertical arrangement of sections. The sections introduce the building, the Romans and Rome, the building work, important parts, the games, the Colosseum today, and a glossary.

pages.text: What Is the Colosseum? The Roman Colosseum was built almost two thousand years ago. It still stands in the center of Rome, the capital of Italy. The Colosseum is about the size of a modern sports stadium. Romans went to the Colosseum to watch different types of games. Men called gladiators fought each other in some games. In other games, men fought wild animals. Sometimes, wild animals were made to fight each other.
pages.brief: The ancient Roman Colosseum stands in the center of Rome, Italy, almost two thousand years after it was built. It is about the size of a modern sports stadium. Inside, men called gladiators fight each other, and other men fight wild animals. In some games, wild animals fight each other.

pages.text: The Romans and Rome Rome once ruled a large empire. Romans fought many battles to defeat other countries and make their empire larger. One emperor of Rome built the Colosseum for the Roman people. He wanted them to enjoy games. He also wanted the building to stand for the power and glory of the Roman Empire. SPAIN.
pages.brief: Ancient Rome rules a large empire. Roman soldiers fight battles to defeat other countries and make the empire larger. One emperor built the Colosseum for the Roman people so they could enjoy games. He also wanted the building to stand for the power and glory of the Roman Empire.

pages.text: Building the Colosseum First, large amounts of soil had to be removed from the ground to build the Colosseum. Then, workers began to build. Workers used wooden cranes to lift and move stones. Much of the building work was done by Jewish people who were enslaved after a war with the Romans.
pages.brief: Workers remove large amounts of soil from the ground to prepare for the Colosseum. Then workers begin to build. They use wooden cranes to lift and move heavy stones. Much of the building work is done by Jewish people who were enslaved after a war with the Romans.

pages.text: Important Parts The Colosseum was made in the shape of an oval. Seats rose in curved rows around an open space where the games took place. The Colosseum had four floors. Arches were built on three of the floors to help hold the weight of the stones above.
pages.brief: The Colosseum is shaped like an oval. Seats rise in curved rows around an open space where the games take place. The building has four floors. Arches are built on three of the floors to help hold the weight of the stones above.

pages.text: Beneath the Colosseum were rooms where people and animals waited to come out to the stadium floor. A cover gave shade to the people watching the games. Wowser! Special lifts raised the gladiators and animals who waited underground up onto the floor of the Colosseum. The door to an animal’s cage and a trapdoor in the Colosseum’s floor opened at the same time.
pages.brief: Beneath the Colosseum, rooms hold people and animals waiting to come out onto the stadium floor. A cover gives shade to the watching people. Special lifts raise gladiators and animals from underground up onto the floor. An animal-cage door and a trapdoor in the floor open at the same time.

pages.text: Violence and the Ancient Romans Violence was an important part of ancient Roman culture. Artwork showing violence appeared in many settings in Rome, including its monuments and public buildings. They served as reminders of Roman might and the power of the emperor. The Games The games at the Colosseum started in the morning. They lasted until darkness fell. In the morning, wild animal parades took place. Sometimes men would fight strong animals like lions and alligators. Other times, animals fought each other. Do You Know? Slavery in ancient Rome was not based on a person’s skin color or where they were from. Most people enslaved by the Romans were taken captive during wartime. Many Roman generals became rich by selling people into slavery after winning a battle.
pages.brief: Ancient Roman culture includes violence, and artwork showing violence appears on monuments and public buildings as a reminder of Roman might and the emperor's power. At the Colosseum, games begin in the morning and last until darkness. Wild animal parades take place, men fight strong animals such as lions and alligators, and animals fight each other.

pages.text: In the afternoon, gladiators fought battles. Gladiators were trained at a special school. Some gladiators had been taken in wars. Others were enslaved people. If they won enough fights, they might win their freedom. Some gladiators were freemen who chose to fight. They wanted glory.
pages.brief: In the afternoon, gladiators fight battles. They train at a special school. Some gladiators were taken in wars, others are enslaved people. If they win enough fights, they might win their freedom. Some gladiators are freemen who choose to fight because they want glory.

pages.text: Gladiators used many different types of weapons and armor. They had to make sure that the crowds watching them saw enough action. Powerful people, such as the emperor, sat in special ringside seats apart from everyone else.
pages.brief: Gladiators use many different types of weapons and armor during the fights. They have to make sure that the crowds watching them see enough action. Powerful people, such as the emperor, sit in special ringside seats apart from everyone else.

Free women and enslaved people watch from the very top. People use eighty arches on the first floor to enter and exit the arena.

pages.text: In the beginning, these games were very popular. However, over time people lost interest in the Colosseum. The building became a ruin. People began to take its stones away to make other buildings.
pages.brief: In the beginning, the games at the Colosseum are very popular. Over time, people lose interest in the Colosseum. The building becomes a ruin. People begin to take its stones away to make other buildings.

pages.text: The Colosseum Today Today, the Colosseum is a ruin from ancient Rome. It is one of the most popular ancient buildings in the world.
pages.brief: Today, the Colosseum is a ruin from ancient Rome. It is one of the most popular ancient buildings in the world. The ancient Roman building is no longer used for games but still stands as a ruin for people to see.

pages.text: The Colosseum has been chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. It is an important and lasting symbol of the ancient Roman Empire. People will be able to visit it for a long time to come.
