books.title: Why We Sleep
books.art_why: The book is about modern sleep science, doctors, babies, athletes and screens, all of which can be shown in real photographs.

pages.text: Introduction It feels great to curl up between soft sheets and slowly drift off into a sound sleep. Getting a good night’s sleep is important. We need sleep to function well. Like food and water, sleep helps keep us healthy and ready to go. Wowser! Did you know that people spend about a third of their lives asleep? That means someone who is seventy- five years old has spent twenty-five years snoozing!
pages.brief: A person curled up between soft white sheets in a bedroom at night, eyes closing as they drift off to sleep. A glass of water and a plate of food sit on the bedside table, the things that keep a body healthy along with rest.

pages.text: What Is Sleep? Falling asleep happens naturally and at regular times. It’s also easy to stop sleeping. A loud noise is often all that is needed to wake a sleeping person. So what is sleep? And what makes us fall asleep? A Greek thinker from long ago believed that eating made people sleep. That idea is not as strange as it sounds. Most people are ready for a nap after enjoying a big meal. Do You Know? The Greek thinker Aristotle believed that after people ate food, warm vapors went to their heads. The vapors then cooled and went to their hearts. This caused people to feel sleepy. While this is not true, how sleepy you feel does depend on the kind of food that you eat. Some foods cause a sleepy feeling. Others, like chocolate, have caffeine. Those foods can make you perk up instead of wind down.
pages.brief: A grown person leans back after a big meal, eyes heavy and ready for a nap. An ancient Greek thinker in a simple robe pictures warm vapors rising from food to a person's head. A bar of chocolate lies on the table.

pages.text: Doctors learned more about sleep in modern times. They studied the brains of sleeping people. The studies showed that the brain does not really shut down during sleep—it just works differently. This discovery led to more studies on sleeping brains.
pages.brief: Modern doctors in white coats stand in a hospital room beside a sleeping patient, studying images of a working brain on a screen. The sleeping person's head rests on a pillow, calm and still.

pages.text: Doctors wanted to know just what causes changes in brain waves. They learned that the body makes a special substance as it uses energy. During the day, more and more of this substance travels to the brain. There, it slows down the parts of our bodies that are active when we are awake.
pages.brief: A person hurries through a busy day of activity, using up energy. By night the special substance the body has made has travelled to the brain, slowing the busy, wakeful parts so the person grows sleepy and still.

pages.text: The Need for ZZZs If our brain doesn’t shut off while we sleep, what does it do? It helps us learn by storing memories. The brain must organize new information we have learned. This happens while we sleep. It’s sort of like cleaning a closet. The brain sets things up to make it easier for us to remember and use what we’ve learned.
pages.brief: A child sleeps deeply under a blanket while the brain sorts the day's new information, tidying it the way a closet is cleaned and organised so things are easier to find and use later.

pages.text: Sleeping helps our body as well as our brain. When we are awake, we use energy. Body cells get worn down. When we sleep, new cells grow. Sleep helps keep the body from wearing down. For this reason, sleep is important to athletes. Whenever they train, they break down cells. They need enough rest to restore their body and make it stronger. This is also the reason that new babies sleep so much. Most babies double their birth weight in five months. Babies can only grow if there is more building-up activity than breaking-down activity.
pages.brief: An athlete trains hard, breaking down body cells, then rests so the body can build them back stronger. Beside them a newborn baby sleeps in a crib, growing fast, doubling birth weight in five months.

pages.text: Sleep also helps us fight sickness and heal wounds. It body’s cells that fight germs. During sleep, the body uses energy to heal instead of using it to play or work. That’s why doctors tell their sick patients to stay in bed and sleep. Sleep Problems There are a number of different sleep problems. Here are three of the best-known ones. • People with insomnia have a hard time falling asleep. Stress and worry may cause insomnia. Bad pain or sickness may make it very hard to sleep. • Narcolepsy is almost the opposite of insomnia. People with narcolepsy may suddenly fall asleep at any time. Some people’s muscles may become weak. This can cause them to fall to the ground and be unable to move. • Sleepwalking is more common in teenagers than adults. Sleepwalkers move about with their eyes open while asleep. They walk, talk, or even do chores. This usually lasts for less than ten minutes. While it is not harmful to wake a sleepwalker, it’s best to lead him or her back to bed.
pages.brief: A sick patient rests in bed with the covers pulled up while the body heals. Around them three sleepers show sleep problems: one lying awake at night, one suddenly asleep, and one walking with eyes open.

pages.text: Sleep Patterns Not all sleep is the same. Sleep goes through different stages. Doctors studied how people move and breathe when sleeping. They also looked at heart rates. They found that these things change as people sleep. Doctors learned that there are two types of sleep. One kind is rapid, or fast, eye movement (REM) sleep. The other kind is non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. NREM sleep has three different stages. The first stage is short. It happens when people first feel sleepy and start to doze.
pages.brief: Doctors watch a sleeping person closely, noting how they move, breathe and how fast their heart beats. Nearby, a person's head nods as they first feel sleepy and begin to doze in the short first stage of sleep.

pages.text: During stage 2 NREM, muscles don’t move much. Sleepers can no longer tell what is going on around them. This is the part of sleep when memories start to be made. Half or more than half of all sleep time is spent in stage 2 NREM sleep. During stage 3 NREM, sleepers begin to dream. The brain keeps storing memories. It is usually very hard to wake someone from this deep sleep. This stage lasts for nearly a quarter of sleep time.
pages.brief: A sleeper lies very still in bed, muscles barely moving, while memories begin to form. Deeper in the same night the sleeper dreams, sunk in deep sleep that is very hard to wake from.

pages.text: REM sleep is different from the other stages of sleep. During REM sleep, the sleeper’s closed eyes move quickly from side to side. It’s as if he or she is watching a ping-pong match. Yet the sleeper’s body is completely still. Muscles are frozen in place during REM sleep. Perhaps that is because people tend to have wild dreams then. Sweet (and Not So Sweet) Dreams We dream when we are in REM and deep sleep. We dream every night, although we don’t always remember our dreams. All dreams are like stories that play out in our mind. Not all of these stories are happy ones. Nightmares are scary dreams that can make sleepers wake up upset. Young children sometimes have bad nightmares called night terrors. Night terrors can cause them to scream and move about without being fully awake. For many years, people have wondered if dreams had secret meanings. Long ago, some people believed they were messages from the gods. Today, some people think that dreams come from our imagination. Others think dreams have hidden messages.
pages.brief: A sleeping person's closed eyes flick quickly from side to side while the body stays completely frozen and still. Nearby, a young child sits up in bed screaming from a night terror, not fully awake.

pages.text: Getting a Good Night’s Rest Many things should happen when our tired head hits the pillow. When they don’t, we can have problems during the day. Too little sleep can make us grumpy. It can also cause us to make more mistakes. We may have a hard time solving problems. Our bodies have a hard time, too. Wounds take longer to heal. We might feel too hot or too cold.
pages.brief: A tired person drags through the day, grumpy and making mistakes, unable to solve a problem. Their body struggles too, a small wound healing slowly, and they shiver and fan themselves, feeling too cold then too hot.

pages.text: It is very important to have good sleep habits. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time each day. This helps keep your body on schedule. You should also limit your screen time. Try not to watch television or use a computer, tablet, or smartphone right before bedtime. Also limit your activity before going to bed. Going for a walk is fine, but avoid a lot of exercise. Good sleep habits keep the body healthy and the mind sharp. Remember, if you don’t snooze, you just might lose!
pages.brief: A child gets ready for bed at the same time as the night before, tablet and television switched off and put away. Instead of a hard workout, they take a calm evening walk before climbing under the covers.

books.title: Sled Dogs to the Rescue
books.art_why: This is a historical 1925 Alaska rescue story, so illustrated scenes suit the blizzard journey and relay.

pages.text: A Terrible Disease In January 1925, sled dog did not survive the journey. Often, the teams raced through Alaska in a medicine had to be warmed by a fire blizzard to save children’s lives. to keep it from freezing.
pages.brief: In deep snow and wind, a sled dog team races through an Alaska blizzard to bring medicine to sick children. At a stop, people hold the medicine close to a small fire so it will not freeze. The exhausted dogs push on through the storm.

pages.text: It started when a disease spread through a small town in Alaska called Nome. Two Native children died, and others got sick. The children needed medicine right away. The medicine that could save the children was in Anchorage, a great distance away.
pages.brief: In a small Alaska town, Native children lie sick in bed while worried adults stand nearby; two children have died. Snow-covered Nome is shown. Far away, a building in Anchorage holds the medicine that could save the sick children.

pages.text: The medicine could be delivered part of the way by train. Even so, it was 674 miles (1,085 km) from the last train stop to Nome. Sled dogs were the best way to deliver the medicine through the snow, but the distance was too far for one team. A sled dog relay was the only hope.
pages.brief: A train stops at the edge of snowy wilderness. From there, a long snowy trail stretches toward Nome. A single sled dog team stands ready, but the distance is too far for one team. People plan a relay of many teams to carry the medicine.

pages.text: The Great Sled Dog Relay More than twenty teams, most led by Native people, would take part in the relay. Each musher would give the medicine to the next team along the way. When the medicine arrived by train, it was handed to the first team. The race was on. The dogs battled through rough wilderness in the bitter cold, and some.
pages.brief: More than twenty sled dog teams, most led by Native mushers, line up across the snowy wilderness. At the train stop, a person hands the medicine to the first musher. Dogs pull through rough, bitter-cold country as teams pass the medicine from one to the next.

pages.text: A famous musher named Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog, Togo, covered the most dangerous part of the run.
pages.brief: A famous musher, Leonhard Seppala, drives his sled dog team along a dangerous snowy route. His lead dog, Togo, runs at the front, guiding the team through the most hazardous section of the relay. Wind blows snow around them.

pages.text: To save time, they raced over an area of frozen sea. The next day, they raced up snow-packed mountains. They covered 91 miles (146 km)—more than any other team.
pages.brief: Seppala’s team races across a flat stretch of frozen sea, ice spreading around them. The next day, the dogs climb steep, snow-packed mountains. Together they cover 91 miles, more than any other team in the relay.

pages.text: The Dogs Deliver The sled dog teams continued their difficult journey. Gunnar Kaasen, another musher, and his lead dog, Balto, left on the second to last leg in a terrible blizzard.
pages.brief: Sled dog teams continue across the snowy trail. Gunnar Kaasen stands on the runners behind his lead dog, Balto, as their team sets out on the second-to-last leg. A terrible blizzard swirls around them, hiding the path ahead.

pages.text: Balto led the team through the storm. At one point, a gust of wind flipped the sled over, and the medicine fell in a snowbank. Kaasen dug it out with frozen hands.
pages.brief: Balto leads the team through a howling blizzard. A strong gust flips the sled over, and the medicine package falls into a snowbank. Gunnar Kaasen kneels in the snow, digging it out with his frozen hands while the dogs wait.

pages.text: When Balto’s team arrived at the hand-off point, the next team was not ready to leave. Balto’s team continued on to Nome instead. Five and a half days after the relay began, Balto’s team delivered the medicine. The children were saved.
pages.brief: At the hand-off point, the next team is not ready to leave. Balto’s team keeps going toward Nome instead. After five and a half days, the dogs arrive with the medicine. The sick children recover, saved at last.

pages.text: After the Race After the race, Togo, Seppala, and their team went all over the United States, drawing large crowds.
pages.brief: After the relay, Togo, Leonhard Seppala, and their sled dog team travel across the United States. They stand with their sled in front of large crowds of people in towns and cities, showing the dogs that helped save Nome.

pages.text: A statue of Balto was built in a city park. Balto and some of his teammates were in a dog show. They were not treated well and were kept in small cages. People gave money to bring the dogs to a zoo in Cleveland, Ohio, where they stayed for the rest of their lives. Balto is famous for his bravery. However, every sled dog on that journey helped save the sick children when there was little hope left.
pages.brief: A statue of Balto stands in a city park. Balto and some teammates are shown in a dog show, kept in small cages. People collect money to move them to a zoo in Cleveland, Ohio, where they live out their lives. Balto is remembered for bravery, and every sled dog on the journey is honored.

books.title: Amazing Antarctica
books.art_why: Antarctica, its wildlife, scientists and ice all exist today and can be photographed

pages.text: North America Africa Antarctica South America Asia Europe Australia The Seventh Continent Give a globe a spin. On it you can easily find six continents: Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Now look at the bottom of the globe. There you will find continent number seven: Antarctica.
pages.brief: A globe photographed against a plain background, turned to show Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. At the very bottom of the globe lies continent number seven, Antarctica, a white icy landmass at the South Pole.

pages.text: For a long time, no one knew Antarctica was there. It was located far from where anyone lived. People did not discover Antarctica until about two hundred years ago. Since then, we have learned a lot about Antarctica.
pages.brief: A far-off icy landmass seen across a wide stretch of cold ocean, empty of people and settlements, lying far from where anyone lives. The remote white continent sits alone at the bottom of the world, unknown to people for a long time.

pages.text: Antarctica is the coldest continent and has the strongest winds. Less rain and snow fall there than in any other continent. Antarctica is also home to some of the most amazing animals in the world.
pages.brief: A windswept Antarctic landscape of ice and snow under a pale sky, strong wind blowing loose snow across the ground. On the ice and in the nearby water are some of the world's most amazing animals, penguins among them.

pages.text: Freezing Antarctica During the winter, Earth’s southern half is turned away from the Sun. For a couple of weeks in June and July— winter in Antarctica—the Sun never rises. For a period in December and January—summer in Antarctica—the Sun never sets. Its location makes the weather almost always cold, icy, and windy.
pages.brief: Earth seen from space with its southern half turned away from the Sun, so Antarctica lies in darkness during winter, when the Sun never rises for weeks in June and July. In summer the same land stays lit, the Sun never setting.

pages.text: The temperature in summer is usually just above 0°C (32°F). In winter, the temperature often drops below –18°C (0°F). The coldest known temperature on Earth was in Antarctica in July 1983. It was about –89°C (–128°F). This cold explains why thick sheets of ice cover much of Antarctica. In some places, Antarctica’s ice is more than 4 kilometers (2.5 mi.) thick.
pages.brief: A vast sheet of thick ice stretching to the horizon, a wall of ice more than four kilometres deep in places, under a freezing sky. The air is bitterly cold, far below zero, and the icy surface glitters in the low light.

pages.text: With all that ice, it might seem surprising that Antarctica is also the driest continent. It gets less than 5 centimeters (2 in.) of rain and snow each year. Water covers most of Earth’s surface, but it is mostly salt water. Most of Earth’s fresh water is frozen in Antarctica’s ice. The ice has built up over many thousands of years. This happens because snow doesn’t melt completely during the summer.
pages.brief: A wide, dry Antarctic snowfield under a clear sky, only a thin layer of snow on the ground. Almost no rain or snow falls here each year, and the ice has built up over thousands of years because summer snow never melts completely.

pages.text: Life on and Around Antarctica The cold, icy, windy conditions have made Antarctica a dangerous place. Only low plants, such as moss, grow on the continent. No trees grow there. Antarctica has only one native insect.
pages.brief: Low green moss growing on cold bare rock in Antarctica, with no trees anywhere nearby. The icy, windy ground looks harsh and dangerous, and a single tiny native insect stands on the rock beside the moss.

pages.text: Almost all plant and animal life on Antarctica is found near the coasts or in the sea. Among the creatures that call Antarctica’s icy waters home are emperor penguins—the biggest penguin in the world. The leopard seal, a fierce predator of the penguin, also lives in the sea. Wowser! A male emperor penguin has a big job when it comes to a baby penguin. It stays on ice and holds an egg between its feet and body for two months. It does not eat and loses almost half of its weight. If the chick hatches before the mother returns, the father stays with the chick. Once the mother comes back, she feeds the chick. The father can finally go to the sea to eat.
pages.brief: Emperor penguins, the biggest penguins in the world, on the ice near the coast, with a leopard seal swimming in the icy sea nearby. A male emperor penguin holds an egg on his feet, and later a mother feeds a fluffy chick.

pages.text: A Playground for Scientists People around the world have worked hard to protect Antarctica’s animals and land. Many countries send scientists to Antarctica to do research. Some are there all year, even in winter. Others are only there in summer. Do You Know? No one country is in control of Antarctica. In 1961, many countries signed an agreement called a treaty. It makes sure no wars happen in Antarctica so scientists can study there.
pages.brief: Scientists in thick cold-weather clothing working outside a research station on the Antarctic ice, some staying all year and others only in summer. Many countries send them, and an international treaty keeps the continent peaceful for study.

pages.text: Many kinds of scientists come to Antarctica to work. Some study its animals. For example, some scientists study what penguins eat.
pages.brief: A scientist in cold-weather gear kneeling on the ice near a group of penguins, watching closely to learn what the penguins eat. Other researchers work nearby, studying Antarctica's animals in the freezing, windy conditions.

pages.text: Other scientists study Antarctica’s ice. They learn about how the ice has changed. Thousands of other people also visit Antarctica each year.
pages.brief: Scientists standing on a wide glacier, studying Antarctica's ice and how it has changed over time. Further away, a small group of visitors in bright cold-weather clothing looks out over the ice, among thousands who visit each year.

pages.text: Conclusion Antarctica is one of the least-known lands in the world. The cold, ice, and rough seas make it a difficult place to explore and study. However, it’s a place of amazing beauty and an important place to protect.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of Antarctica's beautiful icy coast and rough dark sea, with huge icebergs and towering ice cliffs under a pale sky. The remote land looks hard to explore, a place of amazing beauty that people work to protect.

books.title: The Seed Sowers
books.art_why: The book shows real animals, plants, and natural seed-dispersal scenes that can be photographed.

pages.text: Finned Farmers Fall sunlight peeks through the trees and shines on a stream below. A breeze scatters leaves and fruit across the water. Suddenly, a fish breaks the surface to feed. The fish snaps up a floating piece of fruit. Then it disappears beneath the water and swims downstream. It’s easy to see how the trees help the fish, but the fish also helps the trees. By eating the fruit, the fish is spreading the tree’s seeds. It’s one of nature’s seed sowers.
pages.brief: Sunlight filters through trees onto a stream. A breeze scatters leaves and fruit across the water. A fish breaks the surface, snaps up a floating piece of fruit, then swims downstream beneath the water, carrying the tree’s seeds away.

pages.text: Room to Grow Seed sowers are important to plants. Seeds are the way most plants reproduce. All seeds need the same things to sprout and grow. Plants must get enough sunlight, water, and nutrients to thrive. People who grow crops know this. They do their best to make sure their plants get those things. Farmers spread seeds so plants don’t have to compete for what they need. They plant the seeds far enough apart for each plant to thrive.
pages.brief: A farmer works among crop plants, spreading seeds with enough space between them. The plants stand in rows under open sunlight, with soil and water nearby, so each young plant has room to grow without competing for what it needs.

pages.text: Trees and other wild plants need room to grow, too. They can’t depend on farmers to spread their seeds. Instead, wild plants depend on nature to do the job. Some seeds are blown by the wind, while others float away on water. Some seeds are carried off by animals, often on purpose. Animals may hide seeds to eat later, or they may take seeds to feed to their young. Some animals spread seeds without even trying. Many seeds sprout far and wide thanks to animal seed sowers. The word zoo refers to animals. It’s part of the word zoochory. Zoochory is the scientific name for the process of animals spreading seeds.
pages.brief: Trees and wild plants grow in a woodland and open field. Some seeds blow through the air, while others float away on water or are carried by animals. An animal hides seeds to eat later or takes them to its young, and many seeds sprout far and wide.

pages.text: Tasty, Pretty, Wild plants have many ways to get animals to carry their seeds. Some seeds just taste good. Animals seek them out to eat. For example, bears and deer love the taste of acorns. Even if a seed doesn’t taste good to an animal, its fruit might. Papaya seeds taste peppery. The fruit around the seeds, however, is sweet. Animals that eat the fruit sometimes eat the seeds, too.
pages.brief: A bear and a deer search for acorns and eat them. Nearby, a papaya fruit hangs ripe and sweet, while its peppery seeds sit inside. Animals eat the fruit and sometimes swallow the seeds, helping the plant spread.

pages.text: Many plants make fruit or seeds that are easy for animals to spot. Some animals see certain colors better than others. Blackbirds, for example, are attracted to red fruits and berries. Seeds on the ground have a special trick for getting around. Many, such as burrs, have small hooks or teeth. The hooks attach to the hair or fur of passing animals. If you take a dog for a walk through a field in autumn, it may come home covered in burrs. Foxtail grass grows in the western United States. It has spiked seeds that spread by burrowing into the soil. However, the seeds can also spread by hitching a ride on an animal’s fur. The seeds may enter the animal’s ears, mouth, or nose and dig deep inside its body. This can lead to a bad infection or worse if not treated.
pages.brief: A blackbird perches near bright red berries. A dog walks through an autumn field and comes home with burrs hooked in its fur. Foxtail grass grows nearby, its spiked seeds ready to burrow into soil or hitch a ride on an animal.

pages.text: All Kinds of Seed Sowers Some animals seem to be made for seed sowing. Gray squirrels, for example, gather acorns and other large seeds to store for winter. They run through woods or fields and bury their food stash along the way. Squirrels don’t always remember where they put their stash, however. Come springtime, those forgotten seeds sprout, and new trees begin to grow.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel runs through woods and fields, gathering acorns and large seeds. It buries its food stash along the way. Later, in springtime, some forgotten seeds sprout in the soil, and small new trees begin to grow.

pages.text: Insects are also seed sowers. Ants drag seeds to their underground nests. They are only interested in eating the tasty, fatty part of seeds. They leave the rest to sprout and bloom later. Ants till the ground, too. They dig up soil as they hunt for seeds. This improves growing conditions for the seeds they leave.
pages.brief: Ants drag seeds across the ground to their underground nests. They eat only the tasty, fatty parts and leave the rest behind. The ants also dig up and turn the soil as they hunt, making better growing conditions for the seeds they leave to sprout and bloom.

pages.text: Reptiles are seed sowers as well. Giant Galapagos tortoises are amazing seed- spreading machines. They can eat, move, and poop the seeds of more than forty- five plant species. They spread seeds over great distances. Colombia’s green common iguanas do their fair share, too. Iguanas crawl over plants while eating their leaves. Seeds stick to their snout and to a flap of skin hanging from their neck called a dewlap. Later the seeds drop to the ground far from the parent plant.
pages.brief: A giant Galapagos tortoise eats plants and moves slowly across the ground, spreading seeds in its poop over great distances. A green common iguana crawls over leaves in Colombia, with seeds stuck to its snout and the flap of skin under its neck.

pages.text: Nature’s “flying spreaders. In tropical areas, fruit bats are attracted to the smells of mangos and bananas. They feast on these fruits and spread their seeds far and wide. Toucans spread seeds by throwing up! They have large beaks made for cracking the tasty, fatty shells of wild nutmegs. Toucans eat the shells and spit up any seeds they accidentally swallow. Fruit bats are great seed sowers. Scientists are studying how fruit bats can help spread seeds to places where forests have burned or been cut down. Feeding boxes that attract bats are filled with fresh fruit and placed in those areas. Bats eat the fruit and then poop the seeds, providing a low-cost way to get forests growing again!
pages.brief: Fruit bats feast on ripe mangos and bananas in a tropical area, then spread seeds far and wide. A toucan cracks open wild nutmeg shells with its large beak and spits up swallowed seeds. In a burned or cut forest, feeding boxes attract bats that poop seeds and help forests grow again.

pages.text: The Scoop on Poop You may wonder how a seed that is eaten can later grow. The answer is simple— animal poop. Sometimes passing through an animal’s body helps seeds grow faster. One example is the kerer ū (KAIR-uh- Zealand. The grow. First, the bird swallows the large berries of the karaka (KAH-rah-kuh) tree. Then its stomach juices weaken the hard coating of the seeds inside the berries. By the time the bird poops the seeds, their hard shells are gone, and they are ready to grow. Plus, they are sitting in a damp pile of poop, which acts like a rich fertilizer!
pages.brief: A kererū bird swallows large berries from a karaka tree in New Zealand. Its stomach juices weaken the hard seed coatings. By the time the bird poops the seeds, their shells are gone, and the seeds sit in a damp pile of rich fertilizer, ready to grow.

pages.text: Some large animals are great seed sowers because of how much they eat. Elephants have big appetites and poop a lot. They can eat a meal and poop the seeds up to 65 kilometers (40 mi.) away. Where there is elephant poop, there are also dung beetles. The beetles shape bits of poop into balls, roll them away, and lay eggs inside. Within fifteen minutes, a swarm of beetles can cart away half a liter (1 pt.) of poop! The seeds from the elephant’s meal are spread out even more, with help from the beetles.
pages.brief: A big elephant eats a meal and later poops seeds far away, up to 65 kilometers from where it fed. Dung beetles gather around the poop, shape bits into balls, roll them away, and lay eggs inside, spreading the elephant’s seeds even farther.

pages.text: Thanks to the Seed Sowers From elephants to beetles and birds to bats, nature gives us a wealth of seed sowers. They spread seeds near and far, each in their own way. Thanks to them, the world keeps producing healthy environments where both plants and animals can thrive.
pages.brief: Elephants, dung beetles, birds, and bats all spread seeds near and far in their own ways. Around them, healthy environments grow with plants and animals thriving together, showing how many different seed sowers help the natural world.

books.title: Dinosaurs
books.art_why: Dinosaurs and prehistoric events existed long before photography, so drawn reconstruction is needed.

pages.text: The World of Dinosaurs Imagine that you’ve been sent back in time 230 million years. The world looks very different from the one you know. All the land on Earth is one giant continent. Shallow seas cover parts of the ground. The weather is warm, even near the poles. In the shadow of an enormous plant, you hear a noise. Something large is hiding there.
pages.brief: A vast prehistoric landscape 230 million years ago: all land joined as one giant continent, shallow seas spreading across parts of it, warm sky above. Near the poles, plants grow. In the shadow of an enormous plant, a large dinosaur hides, partly seen and heard.

pages.text: You have arrived in the time of the dinosaurs. You are probably familiar with dinosaurs from books and movies. These animals were just one part of an entire ancient world. The age of dinosaurs lasted for about 180 million years. Earth changed a lot during that time. The continents split apart, and the first flowering plants grew.
pages.brief: An ancient dinosaur world during the age of dinosaurs. Dinosaurs of different kinds stand and move among plants while the land slowly divides into separating continents. Early flowering plants grow nearby, and shallow seas lie in the distance under a warm sky.

pages.text: Some kinds of dinosaurs died out, and new ones appeared. Like today’s world, the world of the dinosaurs was a changing place.
pages.brief: A changing prehistoric landscape: one group of dinosaurs fades into the distance while different, newly appearing dinosaurs stand among plants. The ground and plant life look different from before, suggesting a world that keeps changing over time.

pages.text: Meet the Dinosaurs Dinosaurs were a kind of reptile that is now extinct. Dinosaurs stood up off the ground, while other reptiles crawled. They had large eyes and could probably see color. Many scientists think that dinosaurs were faster and more active than other reptiles. With the help of these traits, dinosaurs spread across Earth.
pages.brief: Several dinosaurs stand upright off the ground, not crawling like other reptiles. Their large eyes are visible, and they look alert and active as they move across prehistoric ground. Other crawling reptiles are shown low to the ground nearby, with dinosaurs spreading outward across the scene.

pages.text: At least one thousand species of dinosaurs have been discovered and named, but scientists think far more lived on Earth. Dinosaurs could be as small as a chicken or as large as a school bus. Some grew as long as 39 meters (128 ft.). Everything we know about dinosaurs and their world comes from fossils. A fossil is the remains or print of a plant or animal that was preserved in soil or rock. Scientists have found parts of preserved dinosaur skeletons. They have found only a few whole dinosaur skeletons.
pages.brief: A fossil dig in rock where scientists have found parts of preserved dinosaur skeletons. Only a few whole skeletons lie complete, while most are jumbled pieces. Nearby, dinosaurs of many sizes are imagined, from one as small as a chicken to one as long as a school bus, and a very long dinosaur stretches in the distance.

pages.text: Most of the dinosaur skeletons in museums were put together from parts of many different skeletons. Scientists have also found fossil dinosaur footprints, eggs, and even the contents of dinosaurs’ stomachs. All these things help scientists learn how dinosaurs lived, ate, and died.
pages.brief: Inside a museum hall, a large dinosaur skeleton stands assembled from parts of many different skeletons. Around it are fossil footprints, eggs and the preserved contents of a dinosaur’s stomach. Scientists study these finds, learning how dinosaurs lived, ate and died.

pages.text: A Few Kinds of Dinosaurs Different kinds of dinosaurs lived in different places and at different times. A Tyrannosaurus (ty-ran-uh-SOR-uhs) could never have attacked an Apatosaurus (uh-pa-tuh-SOR-uhs). They lived more than fifty million years apart! Scientists name dinosaurs based on what they looked like and what they ate. Because of this, similar dinosaurs are sorted into larger groups.
pages.brief: A split prehistoric scene separated by time: a Tyrannosaurus stands in one place and an Apatosaurus in another, far apart and never meeting. Other dinosaurs with different body shapes and foods appear in separate settings, grouped together by how they looked and what they ate.

pages.text: Theropods This group of dinosaurs is made up of the scary meat eaters we see so often in movies. One of the largest theropods (THEER-uh-podz), Tyrannosaurus, was up to 6 meters (20 ft.) tall. Another type of theropod was only about the size of a human second grader but ran as fast as a horse.
pages.brief: A group of theropod dinosaurs, fierce meat eaters with big heads and sharp teeth. A towering Tyrannosaurus stands up to 6 meters tall. Nearby, a much smaller theropod, about the size of a human second grader, runs swiftly as a horse across the prehistoric ground.

pages.text: Theropods ran on two legs, and they had big, heavy heads and jaws. A Tyrannosaurus tooth could be as long as a dinner plate. Most dinosaurs in this group had giant hooked claws on their feet to catch and kill their food. They were fierce, and fossil skulls show that they also had large brains, which means they were smart. Scientists think they may have lived in their young.
pages.brief: Theropods run on two legs, their big heavy heads and jaws forward. One dinosaur’s huge tooth is compared with a dinner plate, and giant hooked claws curve on its feet. Their fossil skulls suggest large brains, and the fierce animals are shown active together.

pages.text: Sauropods This next group of dinosaurs included perhaps the largest creatures that ever walked on land. Sauropods (SOR-uh- podz) had large, heavy bodies, legs like tree trunks, and long, slim necks and tails. One type of sauropod may have been as tall as a five-story building. If another type stood on a baseball field, it could stretch from home plate to second base from head to tail.
pages.brief: Enormous sauropods with heavy bodies, legs like tree trunks, and long slim necks and tails. One stands as tall as a five-story building. Another stretches across a baseball field from home plate to second base, its long neck and tail spanning the distance.

pages.text: Most meat eaters a group of these giants. Scientists think that some sauropods may have used their tails as deadly whips. For these dinosaurs, getting enough food was a much bigger problem than staying safe from predators.
pages.brief: A group of giant sauropods stands in a prehistoric landscape. One swings its long tail like a deadly whip. The sauropods are surrounded by plants they need for food, and getting enough to eat is a much bigger problem for them than staying safe from predators.

pages.text: Ceratopsians The members of this next group of plant eaters were smaller than sauropods. Ceratopsians (sair-uh-TOP-see-uhnz) were usually about 3 to 9 meters (10–30 ft.) long. They made up for their size with large fan-shaped crests that protected their heads and necks. The crests could have as many as fifteen horns.
pages.brief: Plant-eating ceratopsians, smaller than the giant sauropods, stand in a prehistoric setting. Their large fan-shaped crests shield their heads and necks, and the crests carry as many as fifteen horns. The animals are about 3 to 9 meters long.

pages.text: Many ceratopsians also had horns on their noses and above their eyes. They had strong parrotlike beaks that could snap tree trunks.
pages.brief: Several ceratopsians stand among trees. Horns rise from their noses and above their eyes, and their strong parrotlike beaks bite into thick tree trunks, snapping them. Their fan-shaped crests frame their heads as they feed.

pages.text: Pterosaurs While not dinosaurs, this group of animals lived during the same time. Pterosaurs (TAIR-uh-sorz) and dinosaurs are both archosaurs, also known as “ruling reptiles.” Birds and crocodiles fall into this group as well. Aside from insects, pterosaurs were the first animals to ever fly. Most of these flyers ate meat. Some caught fish, lizards, and insects while they flew. Others ate dead animals they came across. Pterosaurs were different sizes. Some were only 25 centimeters (10 in.) long from wing to wing, while others had wings as long as a bus.
pages.brief: Pterosaurs fly over a prehistoric landscape at the same time as dinosaurs. Some swoop to catch fish, lizards and insects in the air; another feeds on a dead animal below. Their wings range from only 25 centimeters across to as long as a bus. Birds and crocodiles are shown as distant relatives.

pages.text: The Death of Dinosaurs In time, dinosaurs disappeared from Earth altogether. What happened? Scientists still don’t know for sure. Many think that the crash of an enormous meteorite into Earth was at least partly to blame. The meteorite sent dust and fire into the air. The Sun was blocked out for months. The air became colder. Plants died. Rainwater turned muddy and undrinkable. Both plant eaters and meat eaters could have died from sickness and from not having enough food and water.
pages.brief: An enormous meteorite crashes into Earth, sending dust and fire into the air. The Sun is blocked for months, the air turns colder, and plants die. Rainwater becomes muddy and undrinkable. Plant-eating and meat-eating dinosaurs weaken from sickness and from having too little food and water.

pages.text: Whatever killed the dinosaurs also killed hundreds of other kinds of plants and animals. However, one small group of dinosaurs may have survived. When scientists look at the bones of birds and dinosaurs, they see many things in common. Today, many scientists agree that certain types of dinosaurs later became birds.
pages.brief: After the disaster, hundreds of kinds of plants and animals have vanished. A small group of dinosaurs remains. Scientists compare bird bones with dinosaur bones and see many things in common, imagining certain dinosaurs changing over time into birds.

books.title: Seals, Sea Lions, and Walruses
books.art_why: Real seals, sea lions, and walruses can be photographed today.

pages.text: Meet the Pinnipeds You are sitting on a rock by the seashore. Suddenly, a pair of curious eyes peeks up from the water. As quickly as it came, the animal disappears. You are very lucky—you have seen a seal. Seals, along with sea lions and walruses, belong to a group of animals called pinnipeds.
pages.brief: A person sits on a rock by the seashore, looking out over the water. A pair of curious eyes peeks up from the water. The animal disappears again as quickly as it came. The person has just seen a seal.

pages.text: Pinnipeds are marine, or ocean, mammals. Mammals are animals that breathe air, have fur, and have live babies that drink their mothers’ milk. Pinnipeds include seals, sea lions, and walruses. Their name comes from a Greek word meaning “fin-footed.” Pinnipeds have flippers instead of feet. Pinnipeds are predators, which means they eat other animals.
pages.brief: Seals, sea lions, and walruses appear together as ocean mammals with fur and flippers instead of feet. One breathes air at the surface. A mother feeds her live baby milk. Another pinniped, a predator, catches and eats a smaller animal.

pages.text: Life in the Ocean Pinnipeds spend most of their lives in the ocean. They have flippers and long, torpedo-shaped bodies to help them swim. These features make pinnipeds graceful in the water, but awkward on land. When a pinniped goes underwater, its nose and throat shut automatically. Some seals can hold their breath for over an hour. Elephant seals can hold it for two!
pages.brief: Pinnipeds swim in the ocean with long, torpedo-shaped bodies and flippers. One glides gracefully underwater while another looks awkward on land. A pinniped goes underwater, its nose and throat shut automatically. One seal holds its breath for a long time.

pages.text: Most pinnipeds eat fish, squid, octopus, and shellfish such as shrimp and clams. Pinnipeds must dive deep to find these animals. The Southern elephant seal can dive over 1,500 meters (5,000 ft)! That is deeper than any other mammal can go. Pinnipeds have large eyes that can see in deep, dark water. They have good ears to hear their prey swimming around. They also have sensitive whiskers that can feel an animal swimming by or moving around on the ocean floor.
pages.brief: Pinnipeds dive deep in dark ocean water. One catches fish, squid, octopus, shrimp, or clams. A Southern elephant seal dives far down, deeper than any other mammal. Large eyes see in the dark, good ears hear prey, and sensitive whiskers feel animals swimming by or moving on the ocean floor.

pages.text: Keeping Warm Most pinnipeds live in cold oceans near the North and South Poles. How do pinnipeds keep warm? Many pinnipeds have dense fur with smooth hairs on the top and thick, fluffy hairs on the bottom. The fluffy hairs are waterproof. Pinnipeds also have a layer of fat called blubber that keeps heat inside their bodies. Some pinnipeds have blubber 10 centimeters (4 in) thick.
pages.brief: Pinnipeds live in cold oceans near the North and South Poles. One has dense fur with smooth hairs on top and thick, fluffy waterproof hairs underneath. A layer of fat called blubber inside its body keeps heat in. One pinniped has blubber about ten centimeters thick.

pages.text: Some pinnipeds do not stay in cold areas for the whole year. They migrate, or move, to warmer water during the winter. Other pinnipeds live in warm areas year round. Warm-water pinnipeds sometimes have trouble blubber.
pages.brief: Some pinnipeds migrate, moving from cold areas to warmer water for winter. Other pinnipeds live in warm areas all year round. One warm-water pinniped is shown in warm water; it sometimes has trouble with its blubber.

pages.text: Coming to Shore Pinnipeds come to shore, or haul out, to shed their fur, or molt, and to have babies. Some pinnipeds haul out in large groups, while others come to shore one at a time. A pinniped mother has only one baby at a time. The baby, called a pup, can move around and swim as soon as it is born. But it does not have blubber, and it can’t keep warm in water. It usually stays on land. A baby pinniped drinks its mother’s milk for the first few days or weeks of its life. Pinniped milk has lots of fat—it is more like butter than milk. This helps the pup quickly grow a layer of blubber.
pages.brief: Pinnipeds come to shore to shed fur and have babies. A mother has one pup. The pup can move and swim as soon as it is born, but it has no blubber and cannot keep warm in water, so it stays on land. The pup drinks fat-rich milk that is more like butter than milk.

pages.text: Sea Lions Sea lions get their name because some of them have manes and roar like lions. This fur seal looks like a lion. It is called a “seal,” but it belongs in the same group as sea lions. Seals and sea lions look a lot alike. The easiest way to tell them apart is to look for ears. Only sea lions have ears that stick out. Most “trained seals” at ocean parks and aquariums are actually sea lions. Sea lions swim by moving their long necks and long front flippers. They use their back flippers only to steer. Sea lions can also use their flippers to lift their bodies and “walk” on land.
pages.brief: Sea lions have manes and roar like lions. A fur seal looks like a lion. Sea lions and seals look alike, but only sea lions have ears that stick out. A sea lion swims by moving its long neck and front flippers, steers with back flippers, and uses flippers to lift its body and walk on land.

pages.text: Seals Seals have smaller necks and front flippers than sea lions. They swim by moving their back flippers and hind ends. Seals cannot “walk” on their flippers. Instead, they drag themselves along the ground or crawl like caterpillars.
pages.brief: Seals have smaller necks and front flippers than sea lions. One seal swims by moving its back flippers and hind end. On land, it cannot walk on its flippers. Instead, it drags itself along the ground or crawls like a caterpillar.

pages.text: The biggest pinnipeds in the world are elephant seals. Elephant seals get their name because of their huge size and long noses. Leopard seals are fierce predators. They have big mouths and sharp teeth. They often feed on birds such as penguins. They also attack other seals. Ribbon seals have black fur with white bands. Ringed seals have small, ring-shaped markings.
pages.brief: Elephant seals are the biggest pinnipeds, with huge size and long noses. A leopard seal is a fierce predator with a big mouth and sharp teeth; it feeds on birds such as penguins and attacks other seals. A ribbon seal has black fur with white bands. A ringed seal has small, ring-shaped markings.

pages.text: Do You Know? Walruses Walruses are the only pinnipeds with tusks. They use their tusks to show off to other walruses. They also use them to pull themselves up onto land. Some walruses hook their tusks onto floating ice. Then they relax and sleep.
pages.brief: Walruses are the only pinnipeds with tusks. One walrus shows off its tusks to another. A walrus pulls itself up onto land with its tusks. Another hooks its tusks onto floating ice, relaxes, and sleeps.

pages.text: Walruses have very little fur. Their thick skin and blubber keep them warm. When a walrus goes into cold water, its skin turns pale. This is because all of its blood moves to the inside of its body. When the walrus is warm, its blood moves to the surface again. The walrus turns pink. Walruses like to haul out together in big heaps.
pages.brief: Walruses have very little fur. Thick skin and blubber keep them warm. When a walrus goes into cold water, its skin turns pale as its blood moves inside its body. When it is warm, the blood moves to the surface again and the walrus turns pink. Walruses haul out together in big heaps.

pages.text: People and Pinnipeds People have always hunted pinnipeds. When humans invented large ships and guns, they could hunt and kill many more pinnipeds. Soon, many pinnipeds began dying out. Humans used their fur and skin to make clothing. They ate their meat and burned their blubber as fuel. Only the native people of the far north still hunt pinnipeds. They hunt only what they need to survive.
pages.brief: People have always hunted pinnipeds. With large ships and guns, people could hunt and kill many more. Many pinnipeds began dying out. People used fur and skin for clothing, ate meat, and burned blubber as fuel. Only native people of the far north still hunt pinnipeds, taking only what they need to survive.

pages.text: People around the world worried about pinnipeds. Countries began making laws against hunting them. Many pinnipeds have begun to come back. But some are still in danger. Pinnipeds become caught in fishing nets. Others get sick because of pollution. Pinnipeds have very few predators, besides humans. It is up to us to decide what their future will be.

books.title: About Trees
books.art_why: Trees, leaves, bark and syrup are real things that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction Trees are the tallest living plants. Redwood trees can grow as tall as a 30-story building. Giant sequoias can weigh as much as 3,000 large pickup trucks, making them one of the heaviest living things. Trees also live a long time. Many trees alive today were full-grown long before the United States became a country. But these massive trees share something with all plants—they make their own food.
pages.brief: A grove of towering redwood trees seen from the forest floor, trunks rising out of sight. Beside a colossal giant sequoia, several large pickup trucks sit parked to show its enormous bulk. Beyond them, an old, thick-trunked tree stands in a green woodland, sunlight falling through the high canopy.

pages.text: Leaves Imagine being able to make your own food without cooking or even going to a restaurant! Leaves make food for trees by changing energy from sunlight into food. This important work is done by chlorophyll (KLOR-uh-fill), the green coloring in leaves. Leaves come in all shapes and sizes. Most deciduous (dee-SIJ-oo-us) trees have wide, thin leaves, while most conifers have needlelike leaves. Conifers keep their needles through all seasons. Only the oldest needles fall to the ground. Deciduous trees lose their leaves every fall.
pages.brief: A close view of green leaves on a branch, bright sunlight shining through them. Next to it, wide thin leaves of a deciduous tree spread flat, while a conifer's needlelike leaves cluster along a twig. A few of the oldest brown needles lie fallen on the ground beneath the conifer.

pages.text: In the fall, the leaves of deciduous trees show their true colors. These true colors are yellows, oranges, and browns, which hide under green chlorophyll all spring and summer. We see these colors in the fall after leaves stop making chlorophyll.
pages.brief: Autumn woodland scene: the leaves of deciduous trees turned yellow, orange and brown, filling the branches. Fallen leaves scatter across the ground below the trunks, and a few green leaves still cling nearby, showing the colors that were hidden during spring and summer.

pages.text: Branches Branches are the arms that hold up a tree’s leaves. Branches spread leaves out to get as much sunlight as they can. The leaves give shade to other living things on sunny days. Branches start out as twigs, then they grow thicker each year. As a tree grows, its bark cracks open so the branches and trunk can expand. New bark is always growing under the old, ready to protect the tree. If new bark gets stripped away, a tree can die.
pages.brief: A tree's spreading branches reaching outward, holding leaves up to the sunlight, casting shade on the ground where small plants and a person rest. Nearer the trunk, thin twigs and thicker branches are visible, and the bark shows cracks opening where the trunk and branches have expanded.

pages.text: Trunk Tubes in the tree’s trunk carry water from the roots up to the leaves. They also carry sap, or food, down from the leaves to the roots. These tubes are like highways, carrying traffic back and forth. They are close to the outside of the tree, just under the bark.
pages.brief: A cut section of a tree trunk showing the layers just under the bark, with narrow tubes running up and down the wood. Water travels upward from the roots toward the leaves, and sap moves back down, the tubes packed close to the outside of the trunk.

pages.text: A tree doesn’t need the middle of its trunk to live. The middle is made of rings of old growth, not active highways. That’s why a tree can keep growing even if the middle is hollowed out after a lightning strike. All it needs is enough bark to protect its highways.
pages.brief: A storm-damaged tree with a hollow, blackened middle where lightning struck, the inside open and empty. Around the hollow, living bark and outer wood remain intact, and green leaves still grow on the branches above, showing the tree continuing to grow.

pages.text: Roots Trees need soil to keep growing. Roots are part of the highways. They soak up water and nutrients from the soil. Roots also keep the soil in place when it rains. Without the roots of trees and plants, soil washes away. Trees are stuck in the soil because their roots reach deep into the ground. It’s a good thing they can make their own food, since they can’t move to get it.
pages.brief: Tree roots spreading down into dark soil, gripping the earth. Rain falls on a slope where roots of trees and smaller plants hold the soil in place instead of letting it wash away, and the rooted trunk stands fixed in the ground.

pages.text: Sap Leaves use water plus sunlight and air to make food for the tree. This food is in the form of liquid sugars. Sometimes people eat some kinds of tree sugars for food. You’ve probably had tree sugar for breakfast—pouring it over your pancakes or waffles. Have you guessed what tree sugar this is? It’s maple syrup, and it comes from the food, or sap, of a sugar maple tree.
pages.brief: A sugar maple tree with its trunk tapped, sap dripping into a bucket. In the foreground a breakfast table shows a stack of pancakes and waffles with golden maple syrup poured over them, the bottle of syrup standing beside the plate.

pages.text: Seeds Deciduous trees grow flowers, which make seeds that are inside fruit or nuts. Conifers make cones instead of flowers. The cones do the same job for conifers that flowers do on other trees. They make seeds to grow more trees. Each seed holds its own supply of food to keep it alive until it’s ready to sprout.
pages.brief: Branches of a deciduous tree carrying flowers that have become fruit and nuts, while a conifer nearby holds woody cones among its needles. Seeds lie exposed inside an opened cone and inside a cut fruit, each with its own store of food.

pages.text: Growing How does a tall tree grow from a small seed? The seed soaks up water until it can send out a root. With more water, leaves inside the seed case grow until they push up and out. Once this has happened, we say the seed has sprouted. Now the sprout can make its own food and no longer needs the seed’s store of energy. The seed leaves will make food for the new sprout.
pages.brief: A seed resting on damp soil, split open with a small root pushing downward into the earth. Above it, tiny seed leaves push up out of the seed case, and a small green sprout stands with its first leaves unfolded in the light.

pages.text: Conclusion While trees look like they aren’t doing much, they are working. They make their own food by changing sunlight and air into sugars. This helps keep the air clean, too. Trees are homes and food for birds and other animals. Look to see which animals make homes in trees near your home. Some sap, fruit, and trees. Others eat bark and leaves.
pages.brief: A leafy tree full of activity: a bird at a nest in the branches, a squirrel on the bark, insects on the leaves. Sunlight passes through the canopy, and below, an animal nibbles fallen fruit while another chews a strip of bark.

pages.text: Trees do many things. Tree leaves shade us on sunny days. They also shade new sprouts from the heat of the sun so they won’t burn. Tree roots hold the soil in place that trees and other plants need to grow. From saplings to mighty giants, trees stand tall.
pages.brief: A large tree casting shade on a sunny day, people resting in its shadow. Beneath it, small new sprouts grow protected in the same shade, and its roots hold the soil in place. Nearby, a young sapling stands beside a mighty old giant.

books.title: Deep Inside a Copper Mine
books.art_why: A modern working tour mine in Bisbee, Arizona, with real gear and trams, exists today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Queen Mine Tour parking lot sat virtually empty at 1:30 pm on a hot March day. Mom, Sam, and I were going on a tour of the old Bisbee, Arizona, copper mine at 2 pm. My favorite blue sweatshirt was tied around my waist. Mom said the mine was like Grandma’s house in Tennessee. Not too cold, but not warm. That translated into cool for me. On the tour, I learned that the mine stays at about 47 degrees Fahrenheit. Actually, that is downright cold to me.
pages.brief: An almost empty parking lot outside the Queen Mine Tour building on a hot March afternoon in Bisbee, Arizona. Mom, Sam and the narrator stand together before their 2 pm tour, the narrator's favourite blue sweatshirt tied around the waist, knowing the mine stays about 47 degrees inside.

pages.text: I imagined walking through the front door of the Queen Mine Tour building and seeing a humongous gaping hole in a rock wall. Instead, I saw counters and shelves of gear on my slickers, hardhats, and with lamps. There was an old fireplace spewing heat even though it was hot as the dickens outside. The room even smelled like Grandma’s house. Mom was more right than she thought.
pages.brief: Inside the Queen Mine Tour building, where the narrator had expected a gaping hole in a rock wall. Instead there are counters and shelves stacked with rain slickers, hardhats and lamps, and an old fireplace throwing out heat on a hot day in a room that smells like Grandma's house.

pages.text: What I didn’t realize was that the rain slickers were for us. We had to put them on before going into the mine. I hated the whole idea of putting on a heavy vinyl coat that hardly let you breathe. First, I put on my sweatshirt, then the yellow slicker. It was stiff and made crackly sounds as I shoved my arms through the clammy holes.
pages.brief: The narrator pulls on a stiff yellow vinyl rain slicker over a sweatshirt, shoving both arms through the clammy holes. The heavy coat hardly lets air through and crackles with every movement as it is worn ready for the damp mine.

pages.text: I immediately felt a weight around my waist as the tour guide placed a battery pack around me. He showed me how to clip a lamp to my rain slicker; then, I heard it snap closed. The best part was that I got to wear a hardhat. It almost made the yucky, stiff feeling of the slicker worth the trip.
pages.brief: The tour guide loops a battery pack around the narrator's waist and clips a lamp onto the yellow slicker until it snaps shut. A hardhat is placed on the narrator's head, the best part, almost worth the stiff, yucky slicker.

pages.text: We walked through the building and out the back door to the outside. The sunlight hurt my eyes and made me see stars. My sweatshirt and slicker weighed more than I thought they would. We climbed on board what the tour guide called a man-car. All of the sudden this was getting to be fun. Everyone had to straddle these padded benches in the center of each car like we were riding on the back of one long horse. The guide started up the engine, which sounded like a big lawn mower, and the man-car chugged toward the mine.
pages.brief: Out the back door into sunlight so bright the narrator sees stars. Wearing sweatshirt and slicker, Mom, Sam and the narrator climb into a man-car and straddle the padded benches like riding one long horse. The guide starts the engine and the car chugs toward the mine.

pages.text: We got about 100 feet into the mine when the tour guide stopped. He said that if anyone felt claustrophobic, they could get off and walk back. Mom explained to me that some people are scared of tight places. I have to admit, the tunnel was pretty narrow and stuffy. No one turned back though.
pages.brief: About 100 feet into the mine, the man-car stops. The tour guide explains that anyone feeling claustrophobic can get off and walk back, and Mom says some people are scared of tight places. The tunnel is narrow and stuffy, but nobody turns back.

pages.text: The clang, clang of metal wheels on metal tracks made a racket in the tunnel. The man-car vibrated as the angle going down got steeper. The lamps we clipped to our slickers soon became the only lights in the mine. The man-car stopped on the third floor down. We got off and walked through a side tunnel. This tunnel was wide enough to fit about three people across.
pages.brief: Metal wheels clang on metal tracks and the man-car vibrates as the tunnel slopes steeper. Lamps clipped to slickers are the only light left. The car stops on the third floor down, and everyone walks a side tunnel wide enough for about three people across.

pages.text: The air in the mine smelled and tasted funny. It was like I was breathing bits of the copper. It made my teeth hurt. The air was damp, too. Small patches of mud dotted the dirt floor. I could see why we needed the slickers as water drops fell from the rock above us.
pages.brief: The mine air smells and tastes of copper, making the narrator's teeth hurt, and it feels damp. Small patches of mud dot the dirt floor while water drops fall from the rock overhead, showing why the slickers were needed.

pages.text: The guide told us stories about his work in the mine. He showed us a cage, which is an elevator with wire mesh instead of walls. He said it took miners all the way down to the bottom of the mine. They would cram the elevator full of miners and then go down. Miners really couldn’t be claustrophobic and keep their jobs.
pages.brief: The tour guide tells stories of his work in the mine and shows everyone a cage: an elevator with wire mesh instead of walls. It carried miners crammed full all the way to the bottom, so a miner could not be claustrophobic and keep the job.

pages.text: The guide showed us some holes in the wall. Miners filled the holes with sticks of dynamite and wired them to blow up the rock. The miners would blast the rock at the end of their shift. After a blast, the air would be thick 2 with dust, making the air heavy and hard to breathe.
pages.brief: The guide points out holes in the rock wall where miners pushed sticks of dynamite and wired them to blast the rock at the end of a shift. After a blast the air grew thick with dust, heavy and hard to breathe.

pages.text: We went to another part of the mine before we headed back to the top. This part was a big room with lots of little cubbyholes. The tour guide asked us to shine our lights on different parts of the room. I couldn’t believe it! Every now and then, a light would glance off something with a dull shine. He said that was malachite, a beautiful green mineral often found with copper ore.
pages.brief: In another part of the mine, a big room full of little cubbyholes. The guide asks everyone to shine their lamps on different parts of the room, and here and there light glances off a dull shine: malachite, a beautiful green mineral often found with copper ore.

pages.text: At one point in our tour, the guide had us all turn off our lamps. Oh, my gosh, it was so dark. I had never been in total darkness before. There was absolutely no light. I held my hand right in front of my face and I couldn’t even see it. Just as I was beginning to feel scared, the guide had us turn our lamps back on. Do You Know? The Queen Mine produced 8 billion pounds of copper in its 100 years of operation. The copper came from copper ore, which needs to be smelted before the metal in the rock can be used. Also produced by the Queen Mine were: • 2.8 million ounces of gold • 30 million pounds of lead • 77 million pounds of silver • 371 million pounds of zinc.
pages.brief: The guide has everyone switch off their lamps. Total darkness: the narrator holds a hand right in front of the face and sees nothing, never having been in such darkness before. Just as fear begins, the guide has everyone turn the lamps back on.

pages.text: When we got back to the top and the tour was done, I was happy to feel the sunshine. I couldn’t wait to get out of the slicker, heavy belt, and hardhat. I ditched the gear where the guide said to, then ran to the fire to warm up. I couldn’t believe I was so cold, but I was. Though it was later than when we arrived, it was still a hot 90 degrees outside, and that felt warm against my cold skin. Though I had enjoyed the trip through the mine, I had to admit that being a miner was not the job for me.
pages.brief: Back at the top, sunshine again. The narrator ditches the slicker, heavy belt and hardhat where the guide says, then runs to the fire to warm up, surprised at feeling so cold. Outside it is still a hot 90 degrees against cold skin.
